Not reachable in the shipped keymap: keymap.rs:14 ships spacemacs, where `C-x` is the emacs prefix (spacemacs.rs:65) and opens a submap — the key waits for a second keystroke instead. The capability is present as `g C-x` (vim.rs:894), which the keymap comment calls out deliberately. `C-a` is unshadowed and fully correct, counts, hex and negatives included — the pair is asymmetric. Same category as f/F/t/T being labelled jumps and s/S being sneak: a deliberate default, recorded not argued with.

f/F/t/T are now confined to the cursor's line in the vim preset, per motion.txt "2. Left-right motions" ("These commands move the cursor to the specified column in the current line"). `find_nth_char_on_line` clips the rope scan to [line_start, line_end_char_index) and returns None when the search start is already off that line; `find_char`/`find_char_then` select it via a `line_bounded` flag, the four `vim_find_*`/`vim_till_*` commands are bound in keymap/vim.rs, and `;`/`,` inherit the bound through `apply_find_char`. Verified against nvim 0.12.4: gg0fa on "xbxbxb\nyayaya" stays at 1:1 (pre-fix binary jumped to 2:2), backward `Fb`/`Tb` on a line with no match do not move, and `;` will not repeat onto another line. Count, inclusive landing, count-overflow no-move and f-based `;`/`,` all match (fa, 2fa, 3fa, 9fa, fa;, fa,), as does non-adjacent `t` ("xyzaqa": ta->1:3, 2ta->1:5). helix's own find_next_char keeps the whole-buffer scan for the default preset and emacs zap-to-char stays unbounded.

Two divergences remain. (a) `t` still skips a target that is already adjacent: on "yayaya" from column 0 nvim's `ta` does not move, zmax lands at 1:3. This is not a 'cpo-;' question — cpo-; governs only `;`/`,` repeat of a t search, and nvim's default 'cpo' omits ';', which is why nvim's `ta;` does skip while plain `ta` does not; zmax skips in both. It also breaks 2ta, ta;, ta, and dta (nvim deletes 1 char, zmax 3). (b) A find that matches nothing on the line, or whose count overflows, leaves the width-1 selection intact instead of aborting the operator, so `dfz`, `d9fa` and `gg0 dfa` each delete the character under the cursor where nvim leaves the buffer untouched; zmax autosaves the result. (b) predates this change (the pre-fix binary does the same for dfz) but the new line bound now routes cross-line misses into it. book/src/generated/static-cmd.md is stale for the four new commands.

zmax binds the plain motion to a *labelled* jump (find_char_forward_label / jump_to_char_label), not vim's direct move: `fa` paints a label on every `a` and waits for a label key, where vim moves to the next `a` outright. Verified by driving the binary - after `fa` the cursor is still at 1:1 and the buffer is overlaid with labels; the following key is consumed as a label pick. The operator forms are vim-faithful (df/dF/dt/dT go through find_char_then and match vim byte-for-byte), so this is the plain motion only. Capability present, different model.

vim {motion} takes ANY motion; zmax has no operator-pending mode and enumerates the motions in each operator's submap. Standard motions, text objects (i/a) and marks (`/') work. Verified missing or wrong against vim 9.2 by driving both: d/pat (search) and dn do nothing; d% (matching paren) does nothing; d0 deletes one char too many ('harlie' vs vim's 'charlie'). c{motion}/y{motion} share the submap shape.

`{d,c,y}{/,?}pat<CR>` runs a search as an operator motion. Verified against nvim 0.12.4 by driving both editors.

Working: the base exclusive motion (`0d/charlie` -> "charlie delta echo", per pattern.txt:19 "|exclusive|"); backward `d?pat`; `[count]` (`02d/X`); the character search-offsets `e` (inclusive of the match end, `0d/charlie/e` -> " delta echo"), `s`, and `b[N]`, in both `d` and `c` forms; the no-match abort (`d/NOPE`, `c/NOPE`, `y/NOPE` all leave the buffer intact and set "Pattern not found", confirmed with an `A!!` marker as positive control since zmax autosaves); and `["x]` register routing — `"ay/pat` / `"ad/pat` now deposit the span in the named register instead of clobbering it with the pattern, because the prompt's history register is pinned to '/'.

NOT working: the bare `[±]N` LINEWISE offset is off by exactly one line, in both directions. `0d/gamma/+1` on a 4-line buffer should empty the file but leaves "delta"; `0d/gamma/-1` should leave "gamma\ndelta" but leaves "beta\ngamma\ndelta"; `/+0`, `/1` and `/beta/+2` fail the same way. apply_search_offset lands the cursor on the first grapheme of the offset line, so the span ends at that boundary and extend_to_line_bounds snaps without including the target line.

Separately, `c0` and `y0` gained the `extend_backward_exclusive_vim` step that `d0` already had, so all three now stop before the cursor's character: on "alpha bravo charlie" with the cursor at column 6, `c0` yields "XXbravo charlie", `y0` yanks exactly "alpha ", `d0` yields "bravo charlie". The `y0` change was not part of the original gap list but is confirmed correct against nvim.

Caveat: verified on a HEAD + this-change-only build. The repo working tree does not currently compile (unrelated concurrent edits) and target/debug/zmax predates this change, so this needs a rebuild and re-drive in-tree.

gw{motion} reflows to 'text-width' with the built-in wrapper and, per change.txt:1447, ignores 'formatprg'/'formatexpr' — both driven against nvim: with formatprg=rev and with formatexpr=setline(v:lnum,'XX'), zmax gw produces the same buffer as nvim gw while gq is filtered. The cursor is now restored to the same character in the reflowed text (the old 1:1 collapse is gone): 2G10|gwap, 1G1|/4G20|/3G39|gwap, gw}, gwj, gww, gwgw, gwip and gwG all reproduce nvim's cursor and buffer exactly. Still divergent when the cursor starts on a BLANK: the restore indexes the cursor among the region's non-blank characters, which cannot name a space, so it rounds forward — 1G6|gwap gives 1:7 where nvim gives 1:6 (same for 2G5|, 3G9|, 3G20|, 1G6|gw}), and 4G14|gwap lands 6:1 against nvim's 5:26. {Visual}gw is unchanged and still differs (2G10|Vjgw 4:19 vs nvim 3:20; backwards-linewise and charwise visual also reflow a different region).

'shellxescape'/'shellxquote' wrap and escape the command string on every shell-spawning path, matching nvim's argv byte-for-byte across 14 driven cases. `shellxquote` opens a pair and closes per options.txt:5710 — `(` closes with `)`, `"(` closes with `)"`, any other value closes with itself; `shellquote` always closes with itself (`shellquote="(` gives `"(cmd"(`). `shellxescape` prefixes each listed character with `^` anywhere in the command, and only when `shellxquote` is exactly `(` — under `"(`, `{`, or an empty `shellxquote` it is suppressed. The same quoting now applies to `:!cmd`, `:{range}!cmd` (the filter path), and `:r !cmd`; `:r !cmd` spawns a shell and inserts its output linewise below the current line. Divergence: after `:r` (both `:r file` and `:r !cmd`) zmax leaves the cursor on the original line, where nvim moves it into the newly read text (insert.txt:2093). `:set shellxquote="(` also stores the literal `"(` in zmax, where nvim reads the `"` as a comment and leaves the option empty. 'shellredir' and `!`-as-previous-command inside `:r !{cmd}` are unverified.

vim `ze` scrolls horizontally so the cursor sits at the right edge. zmax binds `z e` to scroll_cursor_to_right_edge (commands.rs:34623, keymap/vim.rs:1158), which sets horizontal_offset = cursor_visual_col - (text_area_width - 1 - sidescrolloff) via saturating_sub, reading 'sidescrolloff' through typed::vim_opt_num. The offset is a pure function of the cursor column, so repeated presses are a no-op (unlike zH's half-screen scroll), and it returns early when soft wrap is on, per scroll.txt "This only works when 'wrap' is off". Verified against nvim 0.12.4 in a pty: with nowrap and the cursor on column 101, `zs` then `ze` leaves the cursor on the rightmost text column in both editors (leftcol = col - (width-1)), idempotent on a second `ze`, and with sidescrolloff=5 both reserve exactly 5 columns to the right of the cursor.

Normal-mode `zs` matches nvim: driven at column 100 on a 300-char line with 'nowrap', zmax scrolls so the cursor sits at the left edge (leftcol 99), same as nvim v0.12.4; `zh`/`zH` also scroll left as vim does. In Visual/Select mode the shipped binary ignores the entire z view family (`zs`, `ze`, `zh`, `zl`, `zH`, `zL`, `zz`, `zt`, `zb`) — `v` then `zs` leaves the view exactly where `v` alone left it, whereas nvim sets leftcol=99 and keeps the highlighted area intact. A source edit adding those keys to the Visual `z` submap (keymap/vim.rs, next to the existing `zf`) is present in the working tree but uncommitted and unbuilt; the tree currently fails to compile for unrelated reasons, so the Visual-mode behaviour is unverified. Rightward horizontal scroll in Normal mode (`zl`/`zL` after `zs`) also appeared not to move the view, unlike nvim's `zL`; not confirmed. 'sidescroll' interaction not probed.

zg/zw write the word (lowercased) to 'spellfile' — the first name only — and zug/zuw remove it by rewriting the file, where vim turns the entry into a comment line. zG/zW/zuG/zuW drive a session-only internal word list that is never persisted; this was verified by driving the binary (]s skips a zG'd word, stops on a zW'd word, and neither the spellfile nor ~/.zmax/spell-bad is touched), so the earlier "zG writes the spellfile" defect is gone. Two parts of the zg entry are still unimplemented: a count does not select the Nth 'spellfile' entry (2zg writes the first file, vim writes the second), and zg in Visual mode adds nothing, where vim adds the selected characters including white space. :spellgood!/:spellwrong!/:spellrare!/:spellundo! exist in source and are registered in TYPABLE_COMMAND_LIST, but are not in any built binary and have never been executed; driving :spellgood! against the shipped binary is a silent no-op. :spellrare and :spellrare! flag words as plain bad — zmax has no separate rare class, so vim's rare highlighting/BAD[rare] classification is not reproduced.
vim `zW` marks a word bad for this session only; zmax binds it to spell_add_bad, which persists. vim.rs:1074 `"W" => spell_add_bad, // zW temporarily bad (approx)`.

Normal-mode zG/zW/zuG/zuW now implement nvim's two-list model correctly and this was confirmed by driving both editors. zG/zW (keymap/vim.rs:1169-1170) add to an in-memory internal word list (spell.rs:327/335) that is never persisted; zuG/zuW (vim.rs:1171-1172 -> spell_undo_internal -> spell::remove_internal, spell.rs:343) clear only that list. zug/zuw still route to spell_undo -> remove_user (spell.rs:351), which touches only the on-disk spell-good/spell-bad files. Driven against nvim 0.12.4 for all eight combinations (zg+zuG, zg+zug, zG alone, zG+zug, zG+zuG, zW+zuw, zW+zuW, zw+zuW), zmax matches the oracle on every one: a zg spellfile entry survives zuG, and a zG internal entry survives zug, exactly as spell.txt:98-104 specifies.

What still differs: the ex-command forms `:spellgood!`, `:spellwrong!` and `:spellundo!` are silent no-ops. Their handlers (typed.rs:39037, :4149, :4230) do call the correct internal-list functions and are registered in the command table, but driving them over a pty produces no state change at all, while the non-bang `:spellgood`/`:spellwrong` work in the same session — so dispatch to the bang variants is broken upstream of the handler. Since nvim documents `:spellundo!` as "Like |zuW|" (spell.txt:144), the ex half of this exact distinction is still unimplemented in practice.

Separately, the on-disk representation differs from vim by design: vim comments out an undone spellfile entry and flags bad words with `/!` in the same file, whereas zmax deletes the line and keeps bad words in a separate spell-bad file. Observable spell state is the same.

vim's `zuG`/`zuW` undo the *temporary* `zG`/`zW`; zmax binds them to spell_undo, the same command as `zug`/`zuw` (vim.rs:1076-1079). Moot in any case while `zG`/`zW` persist the word like `zg`/`zw` — see those specs.

describe-char (C-u C-x =): char glyph + dec/oct/hex code, U+ codepoint, Unicode general-category and block, buffer position; pure builder in zmax-core::cursor_info, unit tested

C-u: arms an emacs prefix argument for the next command - 4, and x4 per repeat (C-u C-u = 16); digits typed after it replace the number (C-u 3 0 = 30). A positive argument becomes the command's count, so C-u 5 C-f moves five characters; commands that branch on the argument's shape read Context::prefix_arg(). Distinct from the vim count: it can be negative, and a bare C-u is distinguishable from an explicit 4

M-0..M-9: numeric prefix argument. EditorView::handle_prefix_key folds the digit in at the alt-digit keys directly (guarded so it never steals a bound chord); by name it arms the argument and the digits typed next build it

For a `fn`/`if`/`for`/`while`/`match`/`impl`/... header (line_opens_block) in a brace language (lang_uses_braces), closes any open `(`/`[` then inserts `{ body }` and drops the caret on the indented body line — e.g. `fn tommy()` -> `fn tommy() {<caret>}`, `while (1)` -> `while (1) {<caret>}`. emacs column-number-mode -> column_number_mode (commands.rs:55890, registered commands.rs:2393). Flips crate::ui::statusline::COLUMN_NUMBER_MODE with fetch_xor and echoes "Column-Number mode enabled/disabled", byte-identical to Emacs's own echo. The per-window statusline (statusline.rs:544 render_position) consumes the flag and reproduces Emacs's four-case mode-line-position structure: both modes on draws " 12:5 ", line-number-mode alone " 12 ", column-number-mode alone " :5 ", and the right-segment guard (statusline.rs:98-109) drops the Position element when both are off. All four states verified by driving M-x in the emacs preset under a pty. DIVERGES: (a) the IDE workbench statusline (ide.rs:2661) draws " {pct}%  {LN} {ln}:{co} " unconditionally and reads neither flag, so on the default UI the toggle prints its message but the column indicator never changes; (b) COLUMN_NUMBER_MODE defaults to true, Emacs's column-number-mode defaults to nil; (c) the M-x picker matches only the snake_case name — Emacs's own "column-number-mode" returns zero candidates.

Ports inverse-add-abbrev (lisp/abbrev.el:413-444) for C-x a i l. The name span comes from abbrev_nth_word_span, a faithful port of (forward-word (1+ (- arg))) / (skip-syntax-backward "^w") / (backward-word 1): verified against emacs 30.2 on "alpha beta gamma delta" for arg=1/2/0/-1 -> beta/alpha/gamma/delta, all matching (C-u and M-- reach it in the emacs preset; in spacemacs, evil shadows both, so use M-<digit>, matching real spacemacs). The prompt is verbatim emacs wording, 'Expansion for Mode abbrev "Foo": '. The definition is keyed on (downcase name), and lookup case-folds like abbrev--symbol (lowercase first, verbatim fallback), so defining on "Foo" and later typing "foo" + C-x ' expands. Redefining an existing name prompts 'Foo expands into "bar"; redefine? (y or n) ' with correct y/n semantics. After defining, the abbreviation standing in the buffer is expanded via abbrev_do_expand.

Diverges from emacs in three ways. (a) The expansion is inserted verbatim; emacs case-adjusts it in abbrev-insert:861-882 whenever the buffer text differs in case from the stored (downcased) symbol -- which is this command's mainline path. Emacs turns "Foo " into "Bar baz " and "FOO " into "Bar Baz "; zmax produces "bar baz " for both. Only all-lowercase abbreviations round-trip identically. This lives in the shared expansion path, so plain C-x ' is affected too. (b) The redefine confirmation is a text-entry minibuffer requiring y+RET; emacs's y-or-n-p commits on the single "y" keystroke (y-or-n-p-insert-y inserts and exits). (c) Mode-local abbrev tables remain process-local (emacs_abbrev.rs:166), so a mode abbrev defined here is lost on restart while the global table persists.

`C-x a l` (add-mode-abbrev) is implemented and driven end-to-end in the spacemacs preset: the expansion is the word before point or the active region, only the name is prompted for (`Mode abbrev that expands into "X": `, abbrev.el:367), the name is downcased before it is stored (abbrev.el:375), redefining an existing name asks `NAME expands into "OLD"; redefine? (y or n)` (abbrev.el:373), a negative prefix argument switches the prompt to `Undefine Mode abbrev: ` and removes the entry (abbrev.el:368), and a positive prefix argument takes N words back. Definitions land in a per-major-mode table keyed by zmax's language id (`.txt` -> `text`), separate from the file-backed global table, matching `only-global-abbrevs` = nil. Known divergences: `only-global-abbrevs` handling is newly written but unverified — the last runnable binary ignores the variable and still defines into the mode table when it is `t`, and the tree does not currently compile, so the reroute to the global table has never been observed; the emacs-style prefix argument (N words, 0 = region, negative = undefine) is only reachable in the emacs preset, since spacemacs normal state has no universal-argument and a bare count is ignored; in the emacs preset the `C-x a` submap is missing while the mark is active, so the region-as-expansion branch is unreachable there; and mode-local abbrev tables live only in memory for the session, where Emacs persists them through the abbrev file.

`C-x C-e` runs `eval_last_sexp` (bound only in the spacemacs preset). It takes the sexp ending at `selection.primary().cursor(text)` — emacs's point, the left edge of the block cursor — so with the cursor on the second `(` of `(+ 1 2)(+ 10 20)` it evaluates the first form and echoes `3 (#o3, #x3, ?\C-c)`, as emacs does. An empty preceding range errors `elisp: end-of-file`, matching emacs's `(end-of-file)` signal.

Integer results are echoed in emacs's `eval-expression-print-format` shape (simple.el:2003) — decimal, then `(#o…, #x…[, ?c])`, sign before magnitude for negatives, `prin1-char` forms `?\C-@` / `?\C-\[` / `?\C-_` / `?\C-?` for the controls and `?\(`-style escapes for `"'();[\]{}`, with the character part dropped past `eval-expression-print-maximum-character` (127). Verified byte-identical to `emacs -Q --batch --eval '(eval-expression-print-format N)'` on GNU Emacs 30.2 for 0, 3, 27, 32, 40, 65, 92, 127, 233 and -5. Non-integers echo the prin1 form alone; there is no `⇒ ` prefix.

Prefix arguments follow `eval-expression-get-print-arguments` (simple.el:2087): any argument other than `nil` or a bare `-` inserts the printed text at point instead of echoing; `nil`/`0` keep the 127 character limit, `-`/`-1` lift it, any other argument suppresses the character form. Driven and matching for no-argument, `M-0` and `M-4`. The `-` and `-1` branches are code-correct but currently unreachable: the spacemacs preset routes no key to `negative-argument` (`M--` falls through as an unbound `<A-minus>`) and `universal-argument` is bound only in the emacs preset, which does not bind `C-x C-e`.

`elisp--eval-defun-1`'s forced re-set (elisp-mode.el:1658) is only matched for `defvar`, and by accident of the evaluator rather than by design: `compile_defvar` (vendor/elisprs/src/compiler.rs:343) emits `SETVAR` unconditionally, so re-evaluating `(defvar v 2)` over `v = 99` yields 2 as in emacs. `defcustom` and `defface` are NOT special-cased and still diverge: re-evaluating a `defcustom` leaves the old value (emacs 2, zmax 99) and re-evaluating a `defface` leaves the old spec (emacs `((t :weight normal))`, zmax `((t :weight bold))`). Both forms do exist in the vendored evaluator — `vendor/elisprs/src/prelude.rs:5615` and `:5625`, a port of custom.el's declaration half — so closing this is a matter of porting `elisp--eval-defun-1`'s `custom-declare-variable` / `custom-declare-face` rewrites here, not vendor work. `NO-TRUNCATE` (the `print-length`/`print-level` lift a `0` argument implies) is also not implemented.

SPC x a | -> align_at_bar, bound on ASCII `|` in the spacemacs/base SPC x a subtree (keymap/vim.rs:2314); the `¦` in DOCUMENTATION.org is an org-table artifact and keybindings.el:712 binds `"xa|"`, so the ASCII-only binding and regex are correct. align_lines_repeat (commands.rs:12163) implements align-regexp's REPEAT=t: it walks column by column, pads each still-matching line's pre-delimiter chunk to max(width)+1 (SPACING 1) and emits the delimiter, so EVERY bar on a line is squared; lines that run out of matches stop contributing width and keep their tail verbatim. align_repeat_region (commands.rs:12253) applies it to the selection and, with no real region, walks outward over the contiguous delimiter-matching lines (funcs.el:1391-1401). Verified in a pty against emacs -Q --batch driving the real spacemacs/align-repeat-bar: on "a | bb | c / dddd | e | ff / xx | ccccc | d" zmax produces "a    | bb    | c / dddd | e     | ff / xx   | ccccc | d", byte-identical to the oracle, from a bare cursor and from an explicit region; a fixture with non-matching lines above and below the block confirms the outward walk stops at the same boundaries Emacs does.

STILL PARTIAL for two reasons. (1) The prefix-arg `after` toggle is implemented (align_at_bar reads cx.prefix_arg(), the after branch pads to the right of the delimiter) but is UNREACHABLE: universal_argument is bound only in the emacs preset (keymap/emacs.rs:142,322) while align_at_bar is bound only in the spacemacs SPC tree, so no preset provides both. Driving C-u, C-u 4, a numeric count, and SPC u before SPC x a | all yield the no-arg output or insert a literal "|", and the oracle's after output ("a |    bb |    c / dddd | e |     ff / xx |   ccccc | d") cannot be produced. Closing this needs a prefix-argument entry point in the spacemacs preset (real spacemacs uses SPC u). (2) Under :keymap vim the SPC leader is stripped (keymap/vim.rs:2794-2810), so the binding is spacemacs-preset-only; arguably correct for a vim preset.

Scope: only align_at_bar was repointed at the repeat engine. The other SPC x a * commands are generated by the same spacemacs|create-align-repeat-x macro with REPEAT=t but remain first-match-only align_region - SPC x a , was observed turning "a, bb, c" into "a , bb, c" and touching no other line. align_repeat_region is reusable for them.

C-h 4 i is emacs `info-other-window` (info.el:780-787), whose interactive spec prompts for a file name only under a non-numeric prefix arg; with no prefix it opens the Info directory Top node in another window, reusing an existing window (display-buffer with `inhibit-same-window`, info.el:826-830) and splitting only when the frame has one window — all three confirmed by driving `emacs -Q -nw` in a pty. zmax's `info_search_other_window` (commands.rs:38822) is now written to match: it renders `(dir)Top` via `render_info_node` (commands.rs:15109, shells `info -o - "(dir)Top"`), then `display_other_window` (commands.rs:15125) focuses an existing non-focused view — splitting only when this is the sole window — and `show_text_in_scratch` replaces that view's buffer; a render failure sets an error and leaves the layout alone, and there is no picker to abort. NOT YET VERIFIED BEHAVIORALLY: the working tree does not compile (unrelated `shell_impl_async` and `ui/merge.rs` errors), and the last built binary predates this change and still shows the old `info --apropos` picker seeded at point, so the three divergences are closed in source only. C-x a i l is bound to inverse_add_mode_abbrev in the emacs preset (keymap/emacs.rs:254, committed in HEAD — not new this round). Driven end-to-end in a pty under `keymap = "emacs"` against GNU Emacs 30.2 as oracle, it matches abbrev.el's `inverse-add-abbrev` (lines 427-444) on four points: it prompts `Expansion for Mode abbrev "<name>": ` per abbrev.el:436; it stores the key downcased per `(define-abbrev table (downcase name) exp)` at :441 (verified observably — defining from `FOO` then expanding a typed lowercase `foo` hits); it runs the trailing `(save-excursion (goto-char end) (expand-abbrev))` at :442-444, replacing the word in-buffer with the expansion; and it honours `(interactive "p")` including negative counts, with C-u 2 / C-u 3 / C-u -1 selecting the same word as the oracle ("EXPANDED two", "XX bb cc", "aa ZZ cc").

Known divergence: the expansion is inserted verbatim. abbrev_do_expand (commands.rs:20739) applies the replacement as a plain Transaction with no case adjustment, so abbrev.el:865-884 — upcase-initials-region/upcase-region when the abbrev name is all-caps, capitalize-first-initial when it merely contains caps — is unported. `hello FOO` yields "hello fungible object" where emacs yields "hello Fungible Object"; `hello Foo` yields "hello fungible object" where emacs yields "hello Fungible object". Only all-lowercase abbrev names round-trip identically.

Unrelated but adjacent: C-e in the emacs preset leaves the cursor on the final character rather than past it (col 1:9 on a 9-char line), so a C-e-then-C-x-a-i-l sequence defines the wrong span ("fo" instead of "foo"). That belongs to the move-end-of-line binding, not to this command — with the cursor at true point-max this command is exact.

`C-x a l` is bound to `add_mode_abbrev` in the emacs preset's INSERT keymap (`C-x a i l` -> inverse), and the command ports abbrev.el's `add-abbrev` prompts and word-extraction faithfully: at an equal point position it reproduces emacs 30.2 byte-for-byte, including trailing whitespace — no-arg takes one word back, ARG>0 takes ARG words back, negative ARG prompts `Undefine Mode abbrev: `, an existing definition prompts `NAME expands into "EXP"; redefine? `, and the name is stored downcased. The region clause (ARG 0 / active region) is implemented and works when the region comes from `C-x h`.

It is NOT reachable the way emacs users reach it: `C-SPC` enters Select mode, whose keymap (keymap/emacs.rs:261-281) binds no `C-x` prefix, so `C-x a l` is inert with a region active. With no user region, ARG 0 silently defines a one-character abbrev from the helix block cursor instead of erroring `The mark is not set now`. `only-global-abbrevs` does not exist, so the redirect to the global table is unimplemented; mode tables are in-memory only (no `abbrev_file_name` persistence) and are keyed by document language / `fundamental` rather than an emacs major-mode name.

Unrelated to this command but affecting its documented workflow: `C-e` (`goto_line_end`) stops one character short of emacs `end-of-line`, so `C-e` then `C-x a l` captures a truncated expansion.

partial: zmax config variables are global, not buffer-local; apropos over the editor config variables

apropos_local_value (SPC h v, default/spacemacs preset; keymap/vim.rs:2395 — the vim preset strips the SPC leader, and selecting it from the command palette silently opens no prompt) prompts "Search for value of buffer-local variable (word list or regexp):", matches the pattern against each buffer-local's printed VALUE only, and renders the hits into an *Apropos*-style scratch buffer.

Three defining behaviours of emacs apropos-local-value are now ported and were verified against emacs 30.2 driven side by side. (a) The pattern is parsed the way apropos-read-pattern (apropos.el:360-373) does: a regexp when it contains one of the characters regexp-quote escapes, otherwise a literal, deduped word list joined into the apropos-words-to-regexp alternation (apropos.el:342), matched case-insensitively. Observed in both: "9." matches the value 92 while "rst" does not match the value rust, and the two-word pattern "tmp rs" hits /tmp/fix.rs while "tmp zzz" does not. (b) Matching is against the value, never the symbol name, per apropos-value-internal (apropos.el:970-985): the pattern "tab-w" returns "No apropos matches" in both, though tab-width is a local in both. (c) A buffer that was never :setlocal'd and has no prop line now yields ten always-present Document-owned locals (buffer-file-name, major-mode, buffer-file-coding-system, buffer-line-ending, indent-tabs-mode, tab-width, indent-width, buffer-read-only, buffer-modified-p, buffer-size) instead of the old "no buffer-local variables" error.

Four divergences remain. (1) Enumeration: emacs mapatoms over every local-variable-if-set-p symbol — 230 in the same buffer, 223 in an untouched one — where zmax has the ten Document-owned entries plus vim_local_opts and file_locals::local_vars; the lists overlap in kind, not in membership. (2) Printed-value dialect: emacs matches prin1-to-string output, so strings are quoted and booleans are nil/t, while zmax matches raw Rust formatting (rust, false, Spaces(4)); the pattern "nil" therefore returns 170 entries in emacs and none in zmax. (3) Regexp dialect: a pattern classified as a regexp is handed to the Rust regex crate, not to emacs's regexp engine, so emacs's backslash alternation differs — "9\|zzzz" returns 3 entries in emacs and none in zmax. (4) Presentation: the scratch buffer is static text with a one-line header, so there is no "Type RET on an entry to view its full documentation" hint and no RET-to-documentation binding, no "matching keywords `(...)':" wording for word-list patterns, no "----------------" entry separators, and no per-entry "Value:" line.

`diary-hebrew-birthday` is ported against cal-hebrew.el:774-799. `DateSpec::HebrewBirthday { birth: Date, after_sunset: bool }` stores a CIVIL birth date and `hebrew_birthday` (zmax-core/src/diary.rs:1384) converts it with `hebrew_from_fixed(rd(birth) + after_sunset)`, matching Emacs's `(calendar-hebrew-from-absolute (+ (calendar-absolute-from-gregorian ...) (if after-sunset 1 0)))`; the three date args follow `calendar-date-style`. The optional 4th AFTER-SUNSET arg parses (absent/`nil` false, `t` true) and shifts the birth one civil day. Results render through `hebrew_birthday_string` as Emacs's `"%s's %d%s Hebrew birthday%s"` with ordinal suffix and a " (evening)" marker on the day-before match, reached from `Entry::display_text`, so all six diary listing commands emit the formatted line. Verified by driving zmax-core against live `emacs -Q --batch`: 23/23 probes match, covering the civil-vs-Hebrew discriminator (civil 1990-04-10 fires 2026-04-01 evening / 04-02 and NOT 2026-07-26), both AFTER-SUNSET shifts, ordinals 1st/2nd/3rd/11th/21st/22nd/31st/36th/100th, American/European/ISO date styles, the leap-year Adar branch (civil 1990-03-12 -> 2027-03-23 evening / 03-24), and the `age > 0` guard.

Not yet observed: the M-x `diary-hebrew-birthday` command itself (zmax-term/src/commands.rs:21623). Its source filters today's HebrewBirthday entries and reports `display_text`, falling back to "No Hebrew birthday today (<hebrew date>)", and the display_text path underneath it is verified -- but the workspace binary could not be built during verification (3 unrelated compile errors in zmax-term from concurrent work, plus a stale prebuilt binary), so the command's live behavior is unconfirmed.

Still divergent, separate spec: `diary-hebrew-yahrzeit` continues to read its args as a Hebrew date, accepts no AFTER-SUNSET, and prints the raw entry text instead of Emacs's "NAME's Nth yahrzeit" formatting.

c_CTRL-B — under the vim/spacemacs presets (`Editor::vim_semantics`, set at zmax-term/src/application.rs:253/:935) C-b moves the cursor to the beginning of the command line, the same as `<Home>`/C-a (zmax-term/src/ui/prompt.rs:1879, `move_start`). Verified against nvim: `:/b/Z/<C-B>s<CR>` on "abc" yields "aZc" in both. Applies to the `/` search prompt as well, since both share `Prompt::handle_event`. Under the helix/emacs presets C-b remains `backward-char` (prompt.rs:1880); `<Home>`, C-a and `<Left>` are unchanged.

c_CTRL-D lists the names matching the pattern in front of the cursor, per cmdline.txt: list_completion_before_cursor (prompt.rs:459) feeds completion_fn the slice &self.line[..self.cursor] instead of the whole line, clears the selection, resets wild_press, and leaves the line untouched. Verified in a pty against nvim 0.12.4: ':setx' with the cursor on the 'x' lists set/setglobal/setlocal (nvim: set/setfiletype/setglobal/setlocal) and leaves the line as ':setx'; before the change the whole-line pattern 'setx' matched nothing and listed nothing. The cursor-at-end control (':set' + C-D) is unchanged and produces the identical list. Enter after C-D executes the typed line, so nothing is selected, and the cmdline_eval short-circuit is kept, so the nested '=' prompt of c_CTRL-\_e still lists nothing. `M-s f C-s` (dired-isearch-filenames) is a port of Emacs's isearch state machine over a character-addressed position space: point is `(row, byte offset into that row's file name)`, and `isearch-cmds`, `isearch-opoint`, `isearch-barrier`, direction and wrap flags are all carried (zmax-term/src/ui/dired.rs:281-314, 1198-1442, router 2767-2830). Verified key-for-key against GNU Emacs 30.2 driving `dired-isearch-filenames` on the same 7-name fixture: every repeated match inside one file name is its own `C-s` stop (a 13-press `a` walk produces the identical row sequence, 3 stops in `aaa.txt`); typing after a repeat re-searches from the near end of the current match, so it fails in place with "Failing" instead of dragging point back to an earlier row; the first `C-r` only reverses direction and re-finds the same match from the other side (`isearch-repeat-on-direction-change` nil); a repeat past the last match fails once and wraps on the next press (`isearch-wrap-pause` t), and the prompt reproduces Emacs's "Failing"/"Wrapped"/"Overwrapped"/"case-sensitive" annotations and the " backward" suffix. `DEL` pops the command stack, `C-g` quits a successful search to the origin and rubs a failing one back to the last success, case folding follows `isearch-no-upper-case-p`, and `C-s` on an empty pattern takes the previous string off the search ring. Still partial on one point: the intra-name offset exists only while a search is live -- Dired's own point is a row, and `begin_input` opens every search at column 0 of the selected row (dired.rs:1121), while Emacs opens at point. So a search that exits with RET in the middle of a name does not hand its position to the next search: emacs `a C-s C-s RET` then a new search and `a` lands on the second entry, zmax re-matches inside the first one. There is no match-count echo, which is correct -- `isearch-lazy-count` is nil by default.

`M-s f C-M-s` (dired-isearch-filenames-regexp) opens an incremental filename search whose pattern is compiled as an Emacs regexp: `emacs_regexp_to_rust` (zmax-term/src/ui/dired.rs:324) escapes bare `(`, `)`, `|`, `{`, `}` to literals and turns `\(`, `\)`, `\|`, `\{`, `\}` into the operators, maps `\<`/`\>`/`\_<`/`\_>` to `\b`, `` \` ``/`\'` to `\A`/`\z`, drops `\=`, treats a backslash inside `[...]` as a literal member, and returns None for a trailing backslash; an uncompilable pattern leaves the state untouched so point holds (dired.rs:1238-1240). `isearch_no_upper_case` (dired.rs:387) implements `isearch-no-upper-case-p` including the `[:upper:]`/`[:lower:]` check and the odd-backslash rule, and feeds `RegexBuilder::case_insensitive` (dired.rs:1182), so smart case applies. Verified against GNU Emacs 30.2 driven in a pty on a six-file fixture: `gamma|beta` and `ap(p)` are literal and fail with the "Failing" prompt while point holds, `gamma\|beta` alternates, `p{2}` is literal where `p\{2\}` repeats, `2$` anchors, `be[` holds point, lowercase `be` folds to reach `abe.txt` while `Be` stays case-sensitive and reaches `zBeta2`, and `C-s` on an empty pattern pulls the previous string off the regexp ring and moves point to it. Still partial: the incremental re-search anchor differs. Emacs re-searches from the search origin on every keystroke, so `beta\|` matches the empty alternative and snaps point to the top of the buffer, leaving `beta\|gamma` on `gamma.txt`; zmax continues forward from the current match and never moves point back, leaving it on `zbeta.txt` -- same keys, same fixture, valid regexp, different file. zmax also omits Emacs's echo-area sub-states "[incomplete input]", "[Trailing backslash]" and the "Pending" prefix (the "Failing" prefix is present and agrees), anchors `` \` ``/`\'` to the file name rather than to the whole dired buffer, and does not translate syntax classes `\sX`/`\SX`, category classes `\cX`/`\CX` or backreferences `\1`-`\9`, which fail to compile and therefore hold point. Unrelated to this spec but affecting which row a search lands on, zmax sorts the listing case-insensitively where Emacs uses byte order.

kmacro-step-edit-macro is ported as a real interleaved stepper, not a stub. All three previously-named gaps are closed, verified by driving target/debug/zmax over a pty in the default spacemacs preset (record `C-x (` xx `C-x )` on "abcdef", then `C-x C-k SPC`): (1) the full kmacro-step-edit-map is honoured -- y/SPC execute, d/n/DEL/C-d skip and advance, f keeps a key without executing it, !/c run the rest, C-k skips the rest but SAVES the accepted prefix (reopen shows [1/1] after y C-k), i/I/r/R/a/A all behave per kmacro.el (I and R consume exactly one key sequence; i and r loop until C-j; a executes the current key before appending; A runs the rest then appends at end), ? toggles the help block without advancing, and an unbound key re-asks at the same index rather than aborting; (2) q and C-g leave already-accepted edits applied while leaving last_kbd_macro unrewritten, matching kmacro.el:1290-1293; (3) the prompt renders as "Macro: <kept> [<pending>] <future>" on the status line with "[n/m] : Next command: <key>" and the response list in the info body.

Two things still differ from emacs. TAB (act-repeat) continues on the repeated KEY rather than the dispatched command, because zmax has no command identity for a dispatched key. This is observable, not hypothetical: emacs binds both C-n and <down> to next-line, so emacs auto-acts the second; zmax executes C-n and then re-prompts at "Next command: down". It only coincides with emacs when the repeated keystroke is the identical key. Second, and outside this command's scope, macro recording keeps the terminating C-x of `C-x )`, so a two-keystroke macro steps as [1/3] with a spurious trailing <C-x>; emacs records two keys ("2*C-d" verified against emacs 30.2). Fixing act-repeat needs command identity plumbed through the compositor dispatch; fixing the trailing key belongs to kmacro_end_macro/record_macro.

Emacs `C-x 4 f` / `C-x 4 C-f` (find-file-other-window). The `C-x 4` submap now exists in the emacs preset (keymap/emacs.rs:210-219) as well as spacemacs (keymap/spacemacs.rs:97-110), with f, C-f, b, 0 and `.`; those five bindings match GNU Emacs 30.2 (`key-binding` confirms each). `find_file_other_window` (commands.rs:55339) was rewritten to look for a view other than the focused one and, when one exists, focus it and build the picker with `Action::Replace` plus a `with_on_abort` that restores the previous focus, falling back to `Action::HorizontalSplit` only when this is the sole window — matching the docstring's "creates a new window or reuses an existing one".

UNVERIFIED AND NOT RUNNABLE: none of this has ever been executed. The built binary predates the edits (C-x 4 is unbound there; the old code still goes 2 windows -> 3, reproduced under pty), and the working tree does not compile, so the reuse path has not been driven even once.

KNOWN DIVERGENCES THAT REMAIN:
- >=3 windows: emacs reuses the next window in cyclic order (verified: with focus on the middle of 3, emacs reused the window below and left the first alone). `views().find(|id| *id != focus)` picks the first view in arena order (tree.rs:608), so with focus off the arena-first view zmax replaces a different window's buffer than emacs. The two rules agree only at exactly 2 windows.
- Focus is moved when the picker OPENS; emacs reads the filename in its interactive spec with the original window still selected and switches only on RET. The abort end-state is restored, but the mid-prompt state differs.
- The workspace picker enumerates existing files, so it cannot visit a not-yet-existing path; emacs's prompt passes `confirm-nonexistent-file-or-buffer` and can.

Partially ported. The four-class `ediff-forward-word` tokenizer (commands.rs:14336-14373) faithfully reproduces `ediff-wordify` — verified against `emacs -Q --batch`, which prints `foo|(|bar|)|baz-qux|12|.5,|hello|!` for `foo(bar) baz-qux 12.5, hello!`, including the `12` / `.5,` split and `$var` staying one token. Two things still differ from emacs. (a) As currently built and shipped, `SPC D r w` replaces both panes with the wordified scratch text (one token per line: `foo`, `(`, `bar`, `)`, `baz`), whereas emacs shows the regions as written and overlays only the differing words; a rewrite to keep the original text and refine inside a changed row exists in the tree but does not compile (`ui/merge.rs:1658`, `String += &String`), so it is unverified and its unit tests have never run. (b) Difference *blocks* are computed line-wise by `align()`, while emacs computes them over the word stream with line structure invisible (`ediff-diff.el:566-575` resolves word indices via `ediff-goto-word` in the original buffer). Emacs reports 0 differences for `"foo bar\nbaz"` vs `"foo\nbar baz"`; a line-wise alignment of the original texts reports one. For multi-line regions the count and boundaries of difference blocks can therefore disagree with emacs even once the within-row refinement lands.

`I` (`dired-do-info`) is bound and reachable. Dired's `handle_event` strips `KeyModifiers::SHIFT` from any `KeyCode::Char` before dispatch, so the uppercase bindings written as bare `key!('I')` fire from a real key press (verified: `I` runs the handler, `C` prompts `Copy to:`, `S` prompts `Symlink to:`). The handler shells `info --file <path> --output -` and shows the captured stdout -- the Top node only -- via `show_text_in_scratch`, then sets `close_requested`, which now pops the Dired overlay from the non-prompt key path so the scratch buffer is left visible and focused rather than hidden behind Dired.

What still differs from Emacs: the result is an ordinary scratch buffer in `plain text`, not `(Info Narrow)`. Emacs's `(info FILE)` builds `*info* (a2ps) Top` with a live navigation graph; here `n`/`p`/`u`/`l`, `Info-menu` and follow-reference do nothing (`n` and `u` leave the cursor at 1:1). Rendering is info(1)'s raw output, so the node header line `File: ...,  Node: Top,  Next: ...` appears as buffer text where Emacs lifts it into a header-line, and menu entries keep their literal `::` where Emacs hides it and makes the entry a link. Closing this needs a per-buffer major-mode keymap mechanism zmax does not have, since binding `n`/`p`/`u`/`l` in a normal document would collide with editing keys.

Separately, the missing-node case is currently invisible: when `info` exits 0 with empty output the code sets the error `info <name>: no such node or anchor: Top`, and Dired correctly stays open, but Dired's own footer occupies the status line so the message is never rendered. Emacs shows `No such node or anchor: Top` in the echo area at once (and without the `info <name>: ` prefix).

LanguageTool via ltex-ls-plus (registered languages.toml:105) is attached to 8 languages: latex (:1464), bibtex (:1479), markdown (:2158), org (:2507), rst (:3770), typst (:4010), asciidoc (:5608) and a new grammarless `text` block (:5827-5833, scope text.plain, file-types txt/text). Verified by driving target/debug/zmax under a pty with a stub LSP on PATH: zmax spawns the server per buffer and sends the id ltex-ls-plus's CodeFragmentizer dispatches on — plaintext for .txt, restructuredtext for .rst (via an explicit `language-id` override, since zmax's language is named `rst`), typst for .typ, bibtex for .bib, markdown for .md — and renders the published diagnostic, statusline going "PROBLEMS ✓" -> "PROBLEMS ⊘1" in every case. ltex-ls-plus is ordered last in each list so the pre-existing primary server (texlab/esbonio/tinymist/marksman) keeps priority; diagnostics from multiple servers coexist rather than clobber (Document::replace_diagnostics evicts only the publishing provider, zmax-view/src/document.rs:3235-3237). Still partial: none of the layer's four key bindings exist. There is no `SPC S` submap in zmax-term/src/keymap/spacemacs.rs — `SPC S` opens the Preferences/Settings UI, so `SPC S l` (toggle LanguageTool for the current buffer) and `SPC S L` (perform corrections) are dead, and zmax has no per-buffer checking toggle at all (`:lsp-stop` stops the server process, a different scope). `[a`/`]a` are taken by goto_prev_parameter/goto_next_parameter (zmax-term/src/keymap/default.rs:118,133), a treesitter motion rather than error navigation; the equivalent capability lives on `[d`/`]d` (:112,127). `ltex-ls` at :104 remains registered but attached to zero languages. All observations used a stub LSP server — the real ltex-ls-plus binary is not installed here, so LanguageTool's grammar-rule behavior and the four newer fragmentizers are unverified.

`C-x w d` (toggle-window-dedication) is implemented in the SPACEMACS keymap only (keymap/spacemacs.rs:555); it is unbound in the emacs preset, where the keys self-insert into the buffer and, because zmax autosaves, write to the file. Dedication is a real tri-state on the view (`View::dedicated_strong`), and the echo string reproduces emacs's own "Window is {no longer|now|now strongly} dedicated to buffer %s" verbatim -- the plain toggle is byte-identical to emacs 30.2. Verified matching: a strongly dedicated window refuses a buffer switch (zmax echoes "Window is strongly dedicated to its buffer"; emacs signals "Window is dedicated to '<buf>'" -- same refusal, different wording), and a weakly dedicated window causes `display-buffer`-style redirection into an existing other window instead of splitting a third, falling back to a split only when no other window exists. NOT matching: the prefix-argument mapping is inverted relative to emacs. emacs gives STRONG dedication only for a raw cons prefix (bare `C-u`) and leaves a NUMERIC prefix weak (`C-u 4` sets dedicated-p=4 and prints "now dedicated"); zmax treats any leading count (2, 4, 16) as strong and a bare `C-u` as plain/weak. Emacs's default `toggle-window-dedicated-flag` value `interactive` -- a third state that auto-clears on a manual buffer switch -- is not modelled.

Missing: a configured notes directory and the note-management commands (new note from the filter text, rename, delete). Zetteldeft's ID/link/tag map is entirely absent

`SPC P /` (spacemacs preset) opens a picker of pandoc input formats seeded from `pandoc --list-input-formats` (51 entries on pandoc 3.10; static reader list when the binary is absent) with the reader inferred from the buffer's language hoisted to the top, then a picker of output formats from `pandoc --list-output-formats`, then runs `pandoc -f <in> -t <out>` over the selection — or the whole buffer when nothing is selected. Output is routed the way pandoc-mode routes it: a text writer's stdout goes to a `*Pandoc output*` scratch buffer (pandoc-mode.el:539 captures stdout into ` *Pandoc output*`) and the source buffer is never rewritten; the file-routed writers get `-o <source>.<fmt>` and only a status line. Verified: markdown->html lands in a scratch buffer with the source byte-identical afterwards; `docx` writes a real 10439-byte "Microsoft Word 2007+" file with no ZIP bytes in any buffer; a non-inferred reader (rst) is honored and its output is byte-identical to the same pandoc invocation; a visual selection converts only that region. Divergences: `epub2`/`epub3` are treated as file-routed and get the format as the literal extension (`doc.epub2`), where pandoc-mode neither file-routes them by default nor would name them that (`pandoc-output-format-extensions` maps both to `.epub`); the scratch buffer is shown immediately, while pandoc-mode leaves ` *Pandoc output*` hidden until `View output buffer`; and there is no persistent per-buffer format/option state, so both pickers are re-asked on every invocation instead of pandoc-mode's sticky transient plus a re-run command. Not ported: 8 of pandoc-mode's 11 main-menu actions — Convert to PDF, View output file, View current settings, View log buffer, the Options subsystem (reader/writer/format-specific/html/epub/citations/math submenus), templates, bibliography, settings files and example lists — and the ox-pandoc org exporter the layer also advertises.
embedded vimlrs (b_assert_beeps): runs {cmd} with errors captured and appends 'command did not beep' to v:errors when it does not error
embedded vimlrs (b_assert_fails): runs {cmd}, matches the captured error against {error}, and appends to v:errors when it does not fail
embedded vimlrs (b_assert_nobeep): the complement of assert_beeps()
`:` opens the command line (command_mode_count, which also takes the count prefix); an empty command line runs nothing, which is the whole of what the spec says `:` does

`:*` is the last Visual area as a range, resolved by the ex range parser (split_leading_range, resolve_filter_range), so every ranged ex command takes it: :*, :*sort, :*normal, :*!cmd, :*m/:*t. Unit test: star_range_is_the_last_visual_area

:lockvar [depth] {name} locks a variable: :let and :unlet on it fail with E741, checked in the command layer that owns both. vim's {depth} is accepted but the lock is on the name (vim's depth 1) - the value lives inside vimlrs and has no lock bit to set
:unlockvar [depth] {name} takes the :lockvar lock off; :let and :unlet accept the name again
c_CTRL-G: next match while 'incsearch' is live (ui/prompt.rs incsearch_cycle). vim presets only - in the Emacs presets C-g stays isearch-abort
c_CTRL-T: previous match while 'incsearch' is live (ui/prompt.rs incsearch_cycle)
dp = :diffput on the change under the cursor - the mirror of `do` (:diffget), which was already bound
i_CTRL-^ toggles 'iminsert', which is the switch the insert-mode self-insert reads before translating a typed character through the :lmap (Lang-Arg) table
c_CTRL-Q: like c_CTRL-V, the next key is data, not a command. vim presets only - in the Emacs presets C-q keeps exiting the completion selection

CTRL-\ e {expr} evaluates {expr} as an EXPRESSION (not a script) and replaces the whole command line with the result, driven and diffed against nvim 0.12.4 in a pty. Verified matching: string literals in either quote style, numbers, floats and dicts; getcmdline()/getcmdtype()/getcmdpos() readable from inside the expression, including type `/` at the search prompt (which zmax words "search:"); the doc's own `getcmdline() .. " Some()"` example; the cursor rule — unchanged mid-line, kept when the result is shorter (clamped to a char boundary), moved to the new end only when it was already at the end, and overridden by setcmdpos(); and the restore path on a failing expression, a syntax error, a reported-but-not-failing error such as `no_such_fn()` (E117), and <Esc>. The resulting line is a real command line: an expression yielding "set nonumber" executes on <CR>.

Still differs from nvim: (1) a nested CTRL-\ e inside the expression prompt is honored instead of being inserted literally — vim types `^\e` into the expression and later executes the original line, zmax clears the expression line and ultimately executes nothing; (2) a List result renders as `[1, 2]` instead of vim's NUL-joined `1^@2^@`.
c_CTRL-] expands the :cabbrev in front of the cursor (zmax_core::abbrev find_expansion, AbbrevMode::Command - the table :cabbrev fills)
c_CTRL-^ toggles 'imsearch', which is the switch ui/prompt.rs reads before translating a typed character through the :lmap (Lang-Arg) table
C-x 5 2: new tty frame (its own window tree and tab set) showing this buffer; only one frame is displayed at a time, as in a terminal Emacs
C-x 5 c: new frame holding a copy of this frame's whole layout - every tab, every split
C-x 5 0: deletes the displayed frame and displays another; refuses to delete the sole frame, as Emacs does
C-x 5 1: deletes every frame but the displayed one
C-x 5 o: displays the next frame (count honoured, wraps) - swaps the live window tree for that frame's
restores the most recently deleted frame; errors when undelete-frame-mode is off, because then nothing was recorded (as in Emacs)
gates whether delete-frame records the frame it deletes; turning it off also drops the recorded frames
picker over the frame names (set by set-frame-name) with each frame's focused buffer; selecting one displays it
renames the displayed frame - the name select-frame-by-name looks up
C-x 5 f: the file picker's open lands in a new frame, via the same pending-display mechanism Emacs's display-buffer uses
C-x 5 r: opens the file in a new frame and marks the document read-only
C-x 5 b: the picked buffer is displayed in a new frame
C-x 5 d: makes a new frame and opens Dired over it; partial because zmax Dired is a modal overlay, so it covers the frame rather than living in a window of it (the same caveat as dired-other-window)
C-x 5 5: arms Editor::pending_display, which Editor::switch consumes on the next buffer display and turns into a new frame
C-x 4 4: the next buffer display is redirected from the current window to a split
C-x t t: the next buffer display is redirected into a new tab
prompts for a buffer name, splits and shows it WITHOUT selecting the window (the difference from switch-to-buffer); with a count greater than one it pops the buffer into a new frame

shows the buffer in another window without selecting it, honouring the other-window/other-tab/other-frame prefix commands. Emacs's display-buffer-alist - the rule list that decides WHERE each buffer goes - is not implemented; zmax splits, or follows the armed prefix

binds $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/zmax/server (else $TMPDIR/zmax<uid>/server), removing a stale socket first, and hands the listener to the event loop, whose tokio::select! accepts on it; run again it stops the server and releases every waiting client. Divergence: the wire protocol is zmax's own line protocol (-auth/-dir/-file/-eval/-nowait), not emacsclient's
C-x #: saves the buffer synchronously, writes 'done' to every client blocked on it, closes their sockets and kills the buffer; with no client waiting it just saves and says so
writes 'abort' to the clients waiting on this buffer and disconnects them without saving
mints 64 characters from /dev/urandom, stores them on the running server and writes them to <socket>.key with mode 0600; from then on a client that does not send '-auth <key>' is refused
connects to another zmax server's socket as a client (reading its .key file if it has one), sends -eval, and reports the reply on the status line

moves point to the last click; the mouse-1 handler in ui::editor dispatches through this command, so it really is the mouse's handler (Editor::last_mouse_pos is the click argument Emacs passes as an event)
the region runs from the drag's anchor to the click; the mouse-1 drag handler dispatches through it, and a non-empty drag leaves the editor in Select mode so operators act on it
extends the region to the click and copies it to the mouse yank register; pressing again at the same position kills it. Bound to mouse-3 through the vim mousemodel=extend path
point moves to the click and the mouse yank register is pasted there; this is what middle-click runs
pastes the primary selection (zmax's mouse yank register, which a drag fills) at point, without moving point to the click
toggles Editor::mouse_wheel_mode, which the wheel branch of the mouse handler reads - with the mode off the wheel really does not scroll
opens the buffer menu (the buffer picker) from the mouse
finds the URL or e-mail covering the last click with zmax_core::goto_address and opens it in the external browser
anchors the secondary selection at the last click. Divergence: not bound to M-mouse-1, which is zmax's add-cursor click; the command takes the click position (or point)

sets the secondary selection from the anchor to the click and paints it with the secondary-selection face text property, so it is visible, survives point moving, and tracks edits through the ChangeSet
inserts the secondary selection's text at the click, leaving the secondary selection itself in place
copies the secondary selection to the kill ring; invoked again with it already saved, it deletes it
overwrite mode that overwrites the newline too, so the file's line layout is preserved
toggles Editor::context_menu_mode, read by the right-button branch of the mouse handler - with the mode off no popup menu appears

text hidden with the invisible text property (hide-ifdef-mode, selective-display, outline folds) is revealed while point is inside it and hidden again when point leaves; the check runs every frame in EditorView::render, the equivalent of Emacs's post-command-hook
when on, the event loop runs desktop-save on quit, writing every file-visiting buffer and its point to the desktop file

toggles the break-indent the document formatter reads, so a soft-wrapped continuation line lines up under the line it wrapped from. Partial: Emacs continues the whole line prefix (indentation AND a comment marker or list bullet); zmax carries the indentation only
every key the editor reads is appended to the named file (an empty name closes it); the hook is in EditorView::handle_event, so it really logs all keyboard input
M-o d: facemenu-set-default - the enriched-mode face map, live once M-x enriched-mode sets the major mode
M-o b: facemenu-set-bold
M-o i: facemenu-set-italic
M-o l: facemenu-set-bold-italic
M-o u: facemenu-set-underline
M-o o: facemenu-set-face (prompts for the face)
C-c TAB: sgml-tags-invisible - hide the markup, show only the text
C-c C-w: fortran-window-create-momentarily (mark column 72 until the next key)
C-c RET: goto-address-at-point - open the URL or e-mail at point in the browser
C-c C-j: term-line-mode
C-c C-k: term-char-mode
C-c C-q: term-pager-toggle
C-c C-c: log-edit-done - handled on its real chord by the commit-message buffer (ui/magit.rs MagitCommit::handle_event)
C-c C-a: log-edit-insert-changelog (same handler)
C-c C-d: log-edit-show-diff (same handler)
C-c C-f: log-edit-show-files (same handler)
C-c C-w: log-edit-generate-changelog-from-diff (same handler)
gud-tbreak. Emacs gives it two keys, C-c C-t and C-x C-a C-t; zmax's C-c C-t is doc-view-open-text, so only the C-x C-a alias is bound
gud-cont. The same split: zmax's C-c C-r is rerun_last_run, so only Emacs's C-x C-a C-r alias is bound
C-x =: what-cursor-position - reports the character at point, its codepoint and its coding
exchange-point-and-mark. In rectangle-mark-mode Emacs cycles the four corners; zmax swaps the selection's ends
SPC f v d: add-dir-local-variable - set a variable for the whole tree in .dir-locals.el
SPC F D: delete all other frames
SPC F O: open a dired buffer in another frame
g@: call 'operatorfunc'. vim applies it to the region the following motion covers; zmax applies it to the current selection (the engine already has that region), so the {motion} argument is not read
M--: negative prefix argument, -1 on its own; digits after it keep the sign (M-- 4 2 = -42), and it flips digits already typed (C-u 5 - = -5)

C-x RET t: sets the coding system the hosted terminal's output bytes are decoded with - ui/terminal.rs transcodes each PTY chunk to UTF-8 with a stateful incremental decoder (a read can split a multi-byte character) before vt100, which assumes UTF-8, parses it. Partial: zmax's OWN tty output is written as &str through the termina backend, which encodes UTF-8 unconditionally and exposes no byte hook, so this governs the terminal zmax hosts, not the outer tty it is displayed on

C-x RET k: sets the coding system typed characters are encoded into on the way to the hosted terminal's PTY (ui/terminal.rs key_to_bytes). Partial, the mirror of set-terminal-coding-system: the outer tty's key bytes are decoded by termina before zmax sees them, so there is nothing there to re-decode

C-x RET x: the coding system the bytes exchanged with the window system's clipboard are in. Read in zmax_view::clipboard::execute_command on both sides - the copy encodes with it, the paste decodes with it - so every command-based provider (pbcopy/pbpaste, wl-copy, xclip, xsel, win32yank) honours it at once

C-x RET X: the same, but consumed by the very next clipboard transfer only. coding::take_selection_coding() TAKES the one-shot, which is what makes it one-shot; the persistent selection coding applies again after

C-x RET p: reads a DECODE ENCODE pair (naming one uses it for both). Read by M-x shell (ui/comint.rs) for its stdout/stderr and its stdin, and by the :sh shell-command family (shell_impl). Fixed a real bug in the same place: comint read its pipes with read_line into a String, which errors on invalid UTF-8, and the error arm ended the reader thread - one stray byte silently killed all further output

C-x RET F: unix file names are bytes, not text, so a name held on disk in a non-UTF-8 coding can only be reached by encoding the typed name the same way. Editor::open now does that (encode_file_name -> OsStr::from_bytes). Windows names are UTF-16 at the API, so there is no byte layer and it is a no-op there

the coding system files are decoded with when opened: threaded into Document::open's encoding argument, which Editor::open had hardcoded to None. Partial: emacs pushes the coding to the front of a PRIORITY LIST its detector still consults; zmax has no multi-candidate detector to prioritise, so the preferred coding is used directly and clearing it restores BOM/charset detection

C-x RET c: arms a coding system for the next file read or write. Consumed by the next Editor::open (C-x RET c latin-1 RET C-x C-f reads that file as Latin-1) or the next Editor::save (C-x RET c koi8-r RET C-x C-s writes the buffer in KOI8-R) - the two uses the manual gives it

a file name decoded with the wrong coding system shows up mojibaked; this runs the same round trip recode-region does (encode back with the wrong coding to recover the bytes, decode with the right one) on the path, and really renames the file on disk, repointing the buffer at it

picks a language environment from a 26-entry table (Latin-1..9, Greek, Hebrew, Cyrillic-ISO/KOI8/ALT, Japanese, Chinese-GB/GB18030/BIG5, Korean, Thai, Turkish, Vietnamese) and sets the file, file-name, terminal, keyboard, selection and process coding systems to that language's coding at once. Partial: emacs's language environments also carry input methods, character sets and sample text; zmax takes the part that has an effect, the coding systems

resolves LC_ALL, then LC_CTYPE, then LANG (the order POSIX resolves them in), reads the codeset after the '.', and applies it as the language environment. Handles the POSIX codeset spellings the WHATWG label table does not know (glibc's eucJP, ISO8859-1)

M-x list-packages: fetches every archive's listing (GNU ELPA, NonGNU ELPA, MELPA) and opens the Package Menu over it. A zmax package is an emacs package: a directory of .el files under ~/.zmax/elpa/<name>-<version>/, put on the elisp load path and evaluated by the embedded elisprs interpreter. The archive-contents parser is a real elisp reader pinned by unit test to the bytes elpa.gnu.org actually serves

downloads <name>-<version>.tar (or .el) over HTTP, unpacks it into ~/.zmax/elpa/, and activates it by evaluating its <name>-autoloads.el (or <name>.el) in elisprs. Dependencies are resolved depth-first from the archive listing and installed before their dependants; 'emacs' is a host-version requirement, not a package, and is skipped, as is anything already installed at a new enough version
installs a package from a local file: a .tar (or .tar.gz - the gzip magic is sniffed) is unpacked as it stands, a bare .el becomes a package of that name versioned 0.0. Then activated like any other

puts every installed package on the elisp load path and evaluates its autoload file. Also runs at STARTUP (Application::load_init_scripts) before init.el, so an init file can configure a package it has installed - which is what package-initialize does in emacs. Only the newest installed version of each package is activated
installs the archive's newer version of one package; errors if the archive has nothing newer than what is on disk
installs a newer version of every package whose status is obsolete (the archive has something newer than what is installed)
writes ~/.zmax/package-quickstart.el, concatenating every installed package's autoload file, so startup does not have to walk the elpa directory - the same file emacs generates for the same reason

re-evaluates every .el file of an installed package and reports the first that fails. Partial, and the reason is stated in zmax_core::package: elisprs is an interpreter, there is no .elc and nothing to byte-compile. What byte-compiling actually CHECKS - that every form reads and evaluates - is what this does (the same precedent as dired-do-byte-compile)
the same for every installed package, reporting how many passed and which failed; same no-byte-compiler divergence
C-h P: shows a package's version, the version installed and where, its archive, kind, home page, maintainer, keywords, dependencies and summary, in a scratch buffer

C-h p: reads a keyword (completed from every keyword the archives' packages declare), filters the package listing to the packages carrying it and opens the menu on the result; refuses a keyword no package has rather than showing an empty list
w in the package menu: opens the :url the archive gives for the package under point in the system browser
RET in the package menu: describes the package under point
i: marks the package under point for installation and steps down, as emacs's marking commands do. package-menu-execute then installs it
d: marks the package under point for deletion and steps down
u (and DEL in the menu, which steps up instead of down): removes the mark from the package under point
U: marks every package the archive has a newer version of for installation - installing the newer version IS the upgrade
~: marks for deletion every installed version that a newer INSTALLED version supersedes (distinct from U, which is about versions in the archive)

x: carries out the marks. Deletions remove the package directory; installations resolve dependencies and go through the download job, then activate. Marks are cleared and the rows rebuilt against what is now on disk, so a row flips available -> installed without a second network round trip
?: shows the package menu's key bindings
H: hides the package under point from the listing
(: shows the packages hidden with H again (greyed), or hides them once more
/ n: narrows the listing to packages whose name contains the text. Filters COMPOSE - each one narrows what the previous left - as they do in emacs
/ d: narrows the listing to packages whose summary contains the text
/ N: narrows to packages whose name OR summary contains the text
/ k: narrows to packages declaring the keyword (the :keywords the archive lists)
/ s: narrows by the Status column - installed, available, obsolete (a newer version is in the archive) or external (installed but in no archive, i.e. from a file or from VC)
/ a: narrows to the packages one archive served (gnu, nongnu, melpa)
/ v: narrows to packages whose version starts with the text
/ m: shows only the packages carrying a mark - what x is about to act on
/ u: shows only the packages that can be upgraded
/ /: drops every filter, restoring the full listing

installs a package straight from its source repository instead of from an archive tarball: git clone into ~/.zmax/elpa/<name>-0.0/, then activate. Shells out to git, the same way zmax_loader::grammar fetches tree-sitter grammars. The result is listed, described, activated and deleted exactly like an archive package
clones a package's source into a directory you name WITHOUT installing it - for working on the package itself
makes an existing working copy an installed package by symlinking it into the elpa directory, so edits to the checkout are live - what emacs does, for the same reason
re-evaluates a VC package's elisp after its source changed and re-activates it. Partial for the same reason as package-recompile: 'built' means byte-compiled in emacs, and elisprs is an interpreter

runs git format-patch over your commits on a VC package, writes the patch series into the package's directory and opens the first. Partial: emacs MAILS the patches to the maintainer, and zmax has no SMTP transport (the same limit message-send documents), so the series is written to disk instead of sent

opens a message-mode draft addressed to the package's maintainer, with the package name, the installed version, its archive, its home page and the zmax version already filled in. Partial: sending queues to the local outbox - zmax has no SMTP transport
a left click moves the cursor to the clicked position (the Down(Left) branch of the mouse handler in ui/editor.rs dispatches through mouse_set_point)

a middle click moves the cursor to the click and pastes there (emacs mouse-2). Divergence from vim's gP: the text comes from the mouse-yank register, not the unnamed one, and the cursor lands after the pasted text
with mousemodel=extend the right button extends the selection to the click, which is vim's own rule for that value; with popup/popup_setpos (the default) it opens the context menu instead
the mouse handler is mode-independent: a left click in Insert moves the cursor to the click and stays in Insert

the wheel scrolls the window under the pointer in every mode, including Insert; the branch calls the same commands::scroll the scroll_down command runs, and honours vim 'mousescroll' (ver:N lines per notch)
as <ScrollWheelDown>, upwards; 'mousescroll' ver:N sets the notch size

the layer's whole job is remapping the command keys for a non-QWERTY layout (bepo, Colemak, Dvorak, Neo). `:set langmap=...` does exactly that - the translation runs before the keymap lookup, so every binding stays reachable

beancount journals get the full layer: tree-sitter grammar plus beancount-language-server. Ledger gets its grammar and indent but no server (none exists), so it is highlighting only. Missing for both: the ledger-mode command surface - reports, register, reconcile, balance - which shells out to the `ledger` binary
zmax reads mail (Rmail, with MIME) and composes it. Missing: maildir support and the `mu` index - mu4e's search query language and its threaded headers view are the layer, and both sit on that index
as mu4e: the reader and composer exist; the notmuch index (and therefore its saved searches, tags and thread view) does not
the mail half is covered by Rmail + compose-mail. Missing: the NNTP newsreader half, and Gnus's group/summary/article three-buffer model
message-goto-followup-to: go to the Mail-Followup-To header, creating it if the draft has none
message-goto-reply-to: go to the Reply-To header, creating it if the draft has none
message-goto-fcc: go to the Fcc header (the file the sent message is copied to), creating it if the draft has none
message-tab: completes the mail alias before point in a header line, an ordinary indent anywhere else (Insert only: in Normal, TAB is vim's jump_forward)
TAB updates the indentation of the current line: c-indent-line-or-region in a C/C++ buffer (Insert only, like Text mode's TAB)

DEL is backward-delete-char-untabify: a tab is first expanded to spaces, so DEL deletes one column of indentation. Bound in the C/C++ overlay (cc-mode reaches it through c-backspace-function); Insert only
major modes redefine TAB: org-cycle in Org, c-indent-line-or-region in C/C++, indent-for-tab-command in Text (keymap/major_mode.rs overlays the language's map on the base one)
major modes redefine DEL: backward-delete-char-untabify in a C/C++ buffer (the base map's delete_char_backward everywhere else)
major modes redefine C-j: tex-terminate-paragraph in TeX, eval-print-last-sexp in Emacs Lisp
mouse-set-point: mouse-1 on text moves point to the click. ui/editor.rs's Down(Left) arm runs this command, so the command really is the handler
mouse-yank-at-click: mouse-2 moves point to the click and inserts the kill ring's top there (ui/editor.rs's Down(Middle) arm runs it)
mouse-save-then-kill: mouse-3 extends the region to the click and copies it; a second press at the same place kills it (ui/editor.rs's Down(Right) arm, under mousemodel=extend)

universal-argument: C-u starts a prefix argument (bare C-u = 4, each further C-u multiplies by 4, digits replace it). Bound in the emacs preset, where C-u is emacs's key; in the shipped spacemacs/vim default C-u keeps vim's half-page-up

digit-argument: M-1..M-9 / M-0 read a numeric prefix argument. The digit is in the keystroke, so EditorView::handle_prefix_key folds it in directly (no keymap leaf can carry it); the command is what M-x digit-argument runs
negative-argument: M-- makes the prefix argument negative (-1 on its own, digits after it build a negative number). Consumed by EditorView::handle_prefix_key, like the digit keys
C-u C-SPC pops the mark ring: set_mark_command asks cx.prefix_arg() and runs pop_to_mark when an argument is present, instead of setting a mark
C-u C-x C-x exchanges point and mark WITHOUT reactivating the region: flip_selections asks cx.prefix_arg() and leaves Select mode when one is present
C-u M-; kills the comment on the line (comment-dwim with an argument): toggle_comments asks cx.prefix_arg() and runs comment_kill when one is present
SPC x A (link-hint-open-all-links): open_all_buffer_links scans the current buffer for URLs and opens each in the OS browser (capped at 50)
SPC x O (link-hint-open-link): link_hint_open_link pickers over the buffer's URLs; confirming one opens it in the browser
SPC x y (link-hint-copy-link): link_hint_copy_link pickers over the buffer's URLs; confirming one copies it to the clipboard register
SPC x Y (link-hint-copy-all-links): copy_all_buffer_links copies every URL in the buffer to the clipboard, one per line

SPC D d d (ediff-directories): ediff_directories prompts for two directories and renders the same-name files that differ, plus files unique to each side, into a scratch overview (top-level, like Emacs)
SPC D d 3 (ediff-directories3): ediff_directories3 prompts for three directories and lists the same-name files present in all three that are not byte-identical
SPC h P s: profiler_start resets and enables the command profiler, which instruments MappableCommand::execute (the single dispatch point) to time every command run
SPC h P k: profiler_stop disables the profiler, keeping its samples for the report
SPC h P r: profiler_report renders per-command call count / total ms / avg µs, slowest first, into a scratch buffer
SPC h P w: profiler_write_report prompts for a path and writes the profiler report text to it

SPC x r ': regexp_generate_strings prompts for a finite regexp and lists every string it matches; enumerate_regex parses a PCRE subset (literals, ( ), |, [ ], ?, {n,m}) and rejects infinite constructs
SPC x r p ': same finite-regexp string generator, PCRE syntax (regexp_generate_strings)
SPC x r e ': regexp_generate_strings_emacs translates Emacs regexp syntax (\( \| \{ \}) to the PCRE subset via emacs_regex_to_pcre_subset, then enumerates
SPC T T (toggle frame transparency): :toggle transparent-background flips the editor's transparent-background option, the terminal's only kind of transparency (the GUI window then shows through)
SPC T B (toggle frame background transparency): :toggle transparent-background, same terminal background-transparency toggle
SPC T f (fringe-mode): toggle_fringe hides/shows the whole gutter column strip (the terminal fringe), stashing and restoring the gutter layout
SPC t m T (toggle mode line itself): :toggle render-statusline turns the per-window status line off/on

SPC q r (restart-emacs): restart_editor refuses on unsaved buffers, else closes every view and sets a flag that main_impl reads after the UI loop exits (terminal restored) to re-exec the binary with the same arguments
duplicate inventory entry for SPC x r ' (generate strings from a finite regexp): regexp_generate_strings
duplicate inventory entry for SPC x r e ' (finite Emacs regexp): regexp_generate_strings_emacs
duplicate inventory entry for SPC x r p ' (finite PCRE regexp): regexp_generate_strings
profile functions/scripts -> command profiler (start/stop/dump)

<S-LeftMouse>: `*` at the click. search_selection_impl expands the bare cursor to the word under it.

<S-ScrollWheelDown>: shift+wheel moves the window one page (inner_height) instead of mousescroll=ver:N lines.

i_CTRL-_: toggle 'revins', gated on 'allowrevins' exactly as vim gates it. Bound to C-_ in the vim preset, where NON_VIM_INSERT frees the key; the shipped spacemacs default keeps C-_ = emacs undo, so this cites the command, not the key.
v_CTRL-G toggles Visual<->Select. zmax has one Select mode (Mode is Normal/Select/Insert), so there is no second mode to toggle to; select_mode is the single mode both map onto.
v_CTRL-O switches Select->Visual for one command. Same single-Select-mode model as v_CTRL-G; no distinct Visual mode exists to switch into.
C-M-y isearch-yank-char: extends the search with the next buffer char (prompt.rs isearch_yank IsearchYank::Char).
C-M-w isearch-yank-symbol-or-char: extends the search with the next word/symbol (prompt.rs isearch_yank IsearchYank::WordOrChar).
C-M-d isearch-del-char: drops the last char of the search string.
C-M-z isearch-yank-until-char: reads a char and extends the search up to it (next_char_handler).
M-s ' isearch-toggle-char-fold: `resume` matches `resume` with accents (IsearchToggle::CharFold).
M-s SPC isearch-toggle-lax-whitespace: a space matches any run of whitespace (IsearchToggle::LaxWhitespace).
M-s M-< isearch-beginning-of-buffer: restart the search from the buffer start, so it finds the first match in the whole buffer.
M-s M-> isearch-end-of-buffer: restart the search from the buffer end, so it finds the last match in the whole buffer.
