Emacs image-crop is an interactive rectangle editor: an SVG rectangle is overlaid on the image and adjusted with mouse-1 drag plus m (move), s (move, square-constrained), RET (execute), q (abort). zmax has none of that - the region must be typed as an ImageMagick WxH+X+Y geometry into an in-mode minibuffer (zmax-term/src/ui/image.rs:146-149, 190-234), because the picture is painted straight to the terminal by an external viewer with no cell to draw a rubber band into. Four concrete consequences, three of them not previously recorded: (1) No display-to-original scaling. image-crop.el computes factor = original_width / displayed_width and multiplies every rectangle coordinate by it before running the command, so the visual selection is always correct under scaling; zmax applies the typed geometry directly to the file's pixel space with no factor (image.rs:360-384), so once `i +`/`i -`…

Carried forward and re-verified from source: (a) the region is typed as a WxH+X+Y geometry into an in-mode minibuffer (`begin_input`, image.rs:151-153) instead of Emacs's SVG rectangle drag session (`image-crop--crop-image-1`) with its own q/RET/m/s loop; (b) the fill colour is an optional second whitespace-separated word (image.rs:353-357) rather than a C-u prefix arg feeding `read-color`; (c) `-fill` precedes `-draw`, so zmax honours a non-default colour whereas Emacs's own command ignores it and always fills black (verified with magick above) — zmax's output differs from Emacs's for any colour but "black"; (d) `image-crop--possibly-rotate-buffer` (ic.el:422) bakes the image's :rotation and :width into the data before the cut, while zmax cuts the untransformed original and applies IMAGE_XFORM only at redisplay; (e) Emacs binds i x via image-map for any image at point, zmax's…

Beyond the admitted "stop re-displays frame 0" (magick 'file[0]', image.rs:462) and the missing image-animate-loop/:index resume: (1) RET can never start or stop a playing animation. The image only exists during a blocking tty handoff — the generated script ends `printf '\n-- %s (Enter) --'; read -r _ </dev/tty` (commands.rs:18292,18298) and drain_tty_command restores the terminal and blocks on Command::status (application.rs:2145) — so while any animation is on screen zmax processes no keys, and the user's Enter is eaten by the shell's `read`. By the time the Image component's RET arm can fire, the terminal has been reclaimed, cleared and re-rendered to the editor (application.rs:2150-2158) and nothing is animating. The toggle therefore only selects which file the NEXT handoff shows, and each press costs a fresh full-screen handoff the user must dismiss with the same Enter key. Emacs…

Three gaps. (1) Backtrace is captured post-return (typed.rs:56800 runs after the call at 56794 has unwound), so the *Backtrace* scratch always shows execute_command -> execute_command_line_inner -> ... -> main, never the frame that raised the error; emacs' debugger is entered inside the signalling frame with live locals. (2) Scope: the hook exists only on the typable dispatcher's Err path, while 743 set_error sites in commands.rs (all key-bound static commands, async/LSP callbacks) and 100 in typed.rs report failures while returning Ok(()), so the flag has no effect on most errors a user can produce. (3) The result is a static, non-interactive scratch buffer (no frame stepping, no eval, no continue) and the state is a private thread_local Cell with no user-visible or settable debug-on-error variable (no :set option, no describe-variable surface).

Three gaps. (a) Effect is not per-buffer text scaling at all: text_scale_increase (commands.rs:38939) bumps one global editor.text_scale counter and emits terminal-wide OSC 50 #+1 (emit_font_step, commands.rs:38926); nothing reads editor.text_scale except the text_scale_set/adjust/mode bookkeeping (commands.rs:61445-61510), no renderer consults it, and emit_font_step's own doc says terminals without a font menu ignore the sequence — so on most terminals C-wheel-up produces only the status line "text scale: +1". The counter is also shared in effect with frame_zoom_in/out (commands.rs:38966+), which drive the same OSC steps, so the two families interfere and text_scale_reset resets globally rather than per window. emacs mouse-wheel-text-scale scales only the buffer in the window under the pointer. (b) Unadmitted runtime shadow: bufferline_y is initialized to 0 (ui/editor.rs:446) and only…

zmax scales the whole terminal, not the buffer. `text_scale_decrease` (zmax-term/src/commands.rs:38947) mutates one global `editor.text_scale` counter and calls `emit_font_step(-1)` (commands.rs:38924-38934) which writes xterm `OSC 50 ;#-1` — a terminal-wide font-menu step, so every window/pane changes together and emacs's buffer-local `text-scale-mode` face-height (two windows at different scales) is unreachable. Terminals with no font menu ignore the sequence, so the command can be a pure no-op while still printing `text scale: -1`. Two further gaps the first skeptic missed: (a) the counter is unbounded while the terminal's font menu clamps at its smallest entry, so `editor.text_scale` desyncs from the real font and `text_scale_apply`/`text_scale_set` (commands.rs:61451-61466), which compute deltas from that counter, then step the wrong amount; (b) the C-wheel branch is only reached…

No SPC D d r chord exists in any shipped preset (vim.rs:266-267 binds only `space D d d` and `space D d 3`); the command is reachable only by name through command_palette. Behaviour also diverges: the output is a static scratch listing, not an interactive per-file ediff session group; revision resolution is git-only (`git diff --name-only HEAD`) rather than the generic VC backend; the listing is recursive while Emacs uses one directory level; DIR resolves against the workspace root (git_exec passes `git -C <root>`); REGEXP is a Rust regex, not an Emacs regexp; empty input errors instead of defaulting to the current directory and a space-containing DIR is unparseable; untracked files are emitted despite the doc comment stating Emacs omits them; and git_exec's `Ok(stderr)`-on-empty-stdout fallback can surface a git warning line as a phantom differing file.

Emacs's interactive spec is (if (eobp) (error "No glyph under point") ...). zmax guards on cursor >= text.len_chars() (commands.rs:42834), but a zmax document…

Data and action match emacs emoji-list (const EMOJI at commands.rs:39034-42808 = 3773 glyph/name/group/subgroup tuples across all 9 Unicode emoji-test groups; on select, insert_at_cursors at commands.rs:46555 applies a real undoable Transaction). Behavioural gaps in the select action itself: (1) emacs emoji-list-select branches on (gethash glyph emoji--derived) and, when derivations exist, opens a second transient chooser WITHOUT inserting -- commands.rs:42864-42871 inserts the base glyph immediately and lists the 1875 skin-tone variants as flat rows, so RET means something different on every derivable entry; (2) emacs calls emoji--add-recent (persistent multisession list, capped at 30) on each insert -- zmax records nothing and has no emoji_recent command in the registry at all; (3) emacs calls barf-if-buffer-read-only first -- insert_at_cursors calls doc.apply directly and…

(1) `SPC i` IS a live prefix in the shipped preset (zmax-term/src/keymap/vim.rs, "Insert" group, `u` => unicode_picker); `SPC i e` is an unclaimed empty slot, so nothing shadows it and the binding was simply never written — no `key:` token exists for this spec. Eight divergences from autorevert.el. Five previously noted: path-keyed global state instead of buffer-local; no undo-boundary around the append; no before-save-hook auto-disable; upstream's trailing (setq auto-revert-mode nil) is not mirrored onto config.auto_reload, so with auto_reload on a whole-buffer reload can race the tail append; the modified-buffer y-or-n-p is absent; plus a toggle-off/on within one 5s tick leaves two concurrent auto_revert_tail_loop tasks racing (commands.rs:14811 only exits when it observes the key missing). Three additional, found here: (1) upstream seeds tail-pos only via (or (local-variable-p 'auto-revert-tail-pos) (setq-local …)) and never unsets it when the mode turns off, so disable then re-enable resumes from the stale offset and appends what was written meanwhile — commands.rs:14796 removes the map entry and 14800 re-seeds from the current file size,…

Reachable only by typing `:org-agenda-file-to-front`; emacs's `C-c [` (org-keys.el:574) is unbound in every zmax preset — the org major-mode table (keymap/major_mode.rs:71-83) has no `[` entry and the tree's only `C-c [` is enriched-mode `:set-left-margin` (major_mode.rs:294). Status message drops emacs's `moved`/`added` word (org.el:15817-15818) and substitutes the canonicalized path in its place, so re-adding an already-listed file is indistinguishable from a first add. TO-END is a positional literal `end` instead of a prefix argument. `ORG_AGENDA_FILES` (typed.rs:8007) is session-local and seeded empty; emacs seeds from persisted `(org-agenda-files t)` and writes back via `org-store-new-agenda-file-list`.

Layer-level: 2 of 3 packages have no counterpart. `request` (http client) is absent entirely, and `evil-goto-definition`'s jump-handler chain is absent - `goto_definition` (zmax-term/src/commands/lsp.rs:1244-1250) delegates straight to LanguageServerFeature::GotoDefinition with no dumb-jump fallback, so `gd` never degrades to grep the way the layer's whole purpose requires. Within dumb-jump: 19 language families vs upstream's 60+; dumb-jump-quick-look, dumb-jump-go-other-window, dumb-jump-back and the xref backend are all missing; multi-candidate results are pushed through the quickfix picker and destructively overwrite the user's quickfix list (qf_set_entries with QfKind::Quickfix, commands.rs:20529); no chord in any preset, reachable only via command_palette or a hand-written keymap. Three code-verified gaps beyond "the chord is unbound". (c) The generation guard does not cover the write it documents. The doc at commands.rs:14633-14635 claims "a quick off/on never leaves two loops writing to the minibuffer", but the liveness check reads generation only before…

Only `:Man-next-manpage` reaches the command. A second `:Man` clobbers the first topic's list, so M-n/`:Man-next-manpage` after two lookups walks the wrong…

M-p is bound nowhere in any shipped preset: emacs.rs:109 gives A-p to goto_prev_diag, and major_mode.rs has no "Man" entry (its only A-n/A-p rows, lines 285-286, are nroff), so the command is reachable only by typing :Man-previous-manpage. There is no Man-mode buffer at all -- man_goto_page (typed.rs:4168) re-renders by spawning `man '<path>' | col -bx` into the run console (typed.rs:4180) instead of narrowing a buffer, so point and scroll position are not preserved. Page state is a single process-wide thread_local MAN_PAGES (typed.rs:4131-4135) rather than emacs' per-buffer Man-page-list/Man-current-page: the command therefore succeeds against a stale list from any buffer instead of being mode-scoped, re-issuing :Man on the topic already displayed resets current to 0 (man_record_pages, typed.rs:4140) so the reader is thrown back to page 1, and only the most recently looked-up topic…

Greedy mode consumes no debug commands at all. Vim keeps debug mode active and sources its debug commands from the normal input stream/typeahead; zmax's flag instead makes `:debug {cmd}` bypass the `>` prompt entirely and run the command immediately (typed.rs:41369-41371), so `q`/`interrupt`/`bt` can never be delivered under greedy — observable as `:debug echo 1` then `q` aborting in vim but executing in zmax. DEBUG_GREEDY has exactly one reader, so `:debug` is its whole effect surface; the existing macro_replaying / feedkeys input paths are not hooked. Additionally `:debuggreedy 0` is accepted as an off-switch (signature positionals (0, Some(1)), typed.rs:55735) though vim's `:debuggreedy` takes no argument.

SPC D m d 3 is bound in no shipped preset — the `space D m` prefix in keymap/vim.rs:360-362 has only `b b`, `b 3`, `f 3` children — so the command is reachable only via the palette (SPC SPC / SPC ?), and the chord string appears in the tree solely inside a doc comment (commands.rs:15761) and a registry description (commands.rs:622). No merge session is created: the command prompts once for "A B ANCESTOR [REGEXP]", then writes a read-only scratch listing splitting the A/B-common names into with-ancestor and without-ancestor buckets and instructs the user to re-run SPC D m f 3 per file, even though three_way_merge is already wired up at commands.rs:61253. Names unique to A or B are dropped instead of being reported as unmatched; MERGE-AUTOSTORE-DIR is unsupported; REGEXP is a fourth whitespace token in Rust regex syntax rather than a separate emacs-regexp prompt defaulted off…

Beyond the poll-only/no-RTM gap: (a) the spacemacs SPC a c s ... path is structurally blocked, not just unbound — vim.rs:1649 binds SPC a c to ai_commit_message as a LEAF, so no chat sub-prefix can exist under it in any shipped preset; (b) no cursor pagination — conversations.list (:40030) and users.list (:39986) are single-shot limit=1000, so on larger teams rooms silently disappear from :slack-select-rooms (making them unselectable for :slack-buffer/:slack-message) and unresolved authors render as raw U-ids via the fallback at :39955; (c) blocking UI-thread network I/O with no timeout — slack_api (:39908) calls ureq send_form synchronously inside the command fn while the adjacent command at :39881 uses cx.jobs.callback, so a hung endpoint freezes the editor uncancellably; (d) :slack-message text is mangled — args are tokenized with quote consumption (command_line.rs:686) then…

The repo's own convention…

Of the 7 chords it installs, `M-S-0` -> windmove_display_same_window is permanently dead: it is stored as Char('0')|SHIFT|ALT while canonicalize_key (zmax-term/src/ui/editor.rs:5128-5136) strips SHIFT from every incoming Char event before keymap lookup, so no keypress can ever match it -- yet windmove_bind reports "7 keys bound". `M-S-f`/`M-S-t` are stored as Char('F')|ALT / Char('T')|ALT and only match on terminals using the legacy encoding; under the kitty enhancement zmax itself pushes, the event arrives as Char('f')|ALT after canonicalisation and misses. Plus: windmove_display (:38140) ignores cx.count, so emacs's prefix-ARG reselect-old-window variant has no path; the four directional commands focus/split immediately rather than arming a deferred display, and a find_split_in_direction miss always splits right/below so left/up land on the wrong side; windmove_display_same_window…
Backspace deletes the char before point (emacs.rs:130).
C-g keyboard-quit -> collapse_selection (emacs.rs:126).
C-j inserts a newline (emacs.rs:149).
DEL deletes the char after point (emacs.rs:129).
:grep <pattern> runs a grep search (typed.rs:13322).

asks what to do about a `.#name` lock another editor holds on this file, then performs the answer: `s` rewrites the lock file to this process (steal), `p` leaves it alone and edits anyway, `q` sets the buffer read-only so the modification cannot land (emacs signals file-locked). With no argument it shows the userlock.el prompt text for the live lock state and reads s/p/q; `:ask-user-about-lock s|p|q` answers directly. Lock detection, staleness (dead pid) and the prompt formatting are in vim_swap.rs; lock files are only written when `:set create-lockfiles=on`

toggles transparent (de)compression of visited files. On (the default, as in emacs), opening .gz/.bz2/.xz/.zst/.Z/.lz/.lzma/.tgz/.txz/.tzst pipes the file through the uncompress program from jka-compr-compression-info-list and puts the plain text in the buffer; saving pipes it back through the compressor, so the file round-trips. auto-mode-alist is matched against the name minus the suffix (strip-extension-flag), so foo.rs.gz opens in Rust. Off, the same file opens as its raw bytes

customizes the bs group that `:bs-show` renders from. No argument lists the variables and their values; `:bs-customize <variable> <value>` sets one and persists it to <config-dir>/buffer_menus for future sessions; `:bs-customize settings` opens the Settings page filtered to bs. Variables: bs-show-flags/-size/-mode/-file (the attribute list), bs-minimal-buffer-name-column, bs-maximal-buffer-name-column, bs-dont-show-regexp, bs-must-always-show-regexp. Regexps and numbers are validated on set

opens the Buffer Menu under the bs settings rather than the C-x C-b defaults: buffers whose name matches bs-dont-show-regexp are omitted unless bs-must-always-show-regexp claims them, the name column is clamped between bs-minimal-buffer-name-column and bs-maximal-buffer-name-column, and only the attributes bs-show-flags/-size/-mode/-file select are drawn. All the Buffer-menu-mode keys (RET/o/2, m/d/s/x/u/U, ~/%/t, S/{/}) work in it

`t` in the Buffer Menu reads the file of the buffer at point as an etags TAGS table and makes it the visited tags table, the same state `:visit-tags-table` sets and the `:tag`/xref lookups read. The file is parsed first, so a buffer that holds no etags entries is refused with a message instead of replacing the working table; a buffer not visiting a file is refused too

toggles the Dired minor mode that repurposes the middle click from dired-mouse-find-file-other-window to dired-mark-for-click, so clicking a line toggles its `*` mark instead of visiting it. Turning the mode off clears every mark and flag (dired-unmark-all-marks), as the emacs mode body does; the command reports which state it left

`I` in Dired runs `info --file <file> --output -` on the file at point and shows the rendered Info text in a scratch buffer, so an Info-format file (including a gzipped .info.gz) is readable from Dired. Not done: there is no Info major mode, so node-to-node navigation (n/p/u/l, following a cross-reference) is unavailable, and the command needs the system info(1) binary

turns Dired click-to-select on (never off) and marks the file the gesture landed on. Emacs binds it to <touchscreen-hold>, which a terminal never delivers, so the file at point — where the hold would have put point — is the one marked

visits the Dired entry at point in another window (a vertical split), the file entered in place when it is a directory. The Dired overlay runs the same code on a middle click, moving point to the clicked row first, and remaps that click to dired-mark-for-click while dired-click-to-select-mode is on

sends the shell-dirstack-query (`dirs`) to the comint shell's subprocess and rebuilds the buffer's directory and pushd stack from the reply, which the reader thread consumes instead of putting in the scrollback. Reports when the shell is not accepting input; needs a live comint shell buffer

toggles the output-side directory tracker: each line the shell writes is matched against dirtrack-list, and the captured group becomes the comint buffer's working directory (a relative capture is resolved against the current one). This is the alternative to shell-dirtrack-mode, which watches the cd/pushd/popd you type

adds every file directly in the directory to the file-name cache, keyed by bare name -> the directories holding it. Subdirectories are skipped, file-cache-filter-regexps (emacs's shipped list: ~$, .o, .exe, .a, .elc, ,v, .class, #$, /.#) are applied, and an optional second argument is a regexp only matching names are added under. Prompts for the directory when called with no argument. `:file-cache-add-directory-using-find` walks nested subdirectories, `:file-cache-add-file`, `:file-cache-clear-cache` and `:file-cache-display` are the rest of the set; the cache is session-only, as in emacs

completes the file name in the open minibuffer from the file-name cache and does emacs's two substitutions in order: first the non-directory part is extended to the longest prefix the cached names share (reporting `complete, but not unique` and listing the alternatives in the completion menu), then, once the name is settled, each repeat cycles through the directories that name was cached in, wrapping at the end and showing `[n of total]`. An uncached name reports [No match]

toggles the dimming of the leading part of a typed file name that its later components override — the part before a `//` or a second absolute name, which resolving the name throws away. On by default, as in emacs; turning it off shows the whole line as live input

adds the current buffer's file to the named fileset, creating the fileset when there is none (emacs asks; naming a new set is the answer). Prompts for the name with no argument, reports when the file is already in the set, refuses a :pattern fileset as emacs does, and persists the change to <config-dir>/filesets. Requires `:filesets-init` first

loads the saved fileset list from <config-dir>/filesets and arms the fileset commands — the other commands refuse until it has run, as emacs's do without (filesets-init) in the init file. Re-running re-reads the store. The set is then operated on as a group: `:filesets-open` visits every file, `:filesets-close` kills the unmodified buffers visiting them, `:filesets-run-cmd` runs a shell command once per file, `:filesets-list` shows the definitions, `:filesets-define-pattern` defines the regexp kind and `:filesets-delete` removes one

removes the current buffer's file from the named fileset and persists the change. Prompts for the name with no argument, reports when the file was not in the set, and errors on an unknown fileset or a :pattern one (which has no explicit file list to edit)

toggles MSB and persists it. With it on, mouse-buffer-menu (bound to C-F10) lists the buffers grouped by major mode — file-visiting buffers first, then by mode, then by name, with the mode as its own column — instead of the plain most-recently-used buffer picker. Not done: emacs's MSB also rewrites the menu-bar Buffer menu, and zmax has no menu bar; the grouping is a sort plus a mode column rather than msb's per-mode submenus, which a terminal picker has no equivalent for

sets up file shadowing: reads the shadow groups and clusters from <config-dir>/shadows and the pending copies from <config-dir>/shadow_todo, and arms the save hook (emacs's shadow-add-to-todo on write-file-functions) that queues a shadowed file's copies when it is saved. Nothing shadows before it has run. `:shadow-define-literal-group` and `:shadow-define-regexp-group` define groups, `:shadow-define-cluster` names a site, `:shadow-copy-files` performs the pending copies (a failed one stays queued), `:shadow-cancel` drops them and `:shadow-shadows` shows where this file is shadowed to. A site here is a directory prefix rather than a Tramp host, since zmax has no Tramp

toggles (or sets with on/off) whether `pushd +n` typed at the comint shell pops the n-th entry to the top of the tracked directory stack instead of rotating the stack around it — tcsh's option. Applies to the live shell and, as a defcustom does, to the shells opened afterwards

toggles (or sets with on/off) whether `pushd <dir>` typed at the comint shell only stacks the directory it left when that directory is not on the stack already — tcsh's option. Applies to the live shell and to the shells opened afterwards

toggles (or sets with on/off) whether a bare `pushd` typed at the comint shell behaves as `pushd ~` instead of swapping the working directory with the top of the stack — tcsh's option. Applies to the live shell and to the shells opened afterwards

mouse-buffer-menu — the buffer menu reached without the keyboard — is on C-F10, emacs's other binding for the same command, and honours msb-mode. Not done on C-mouse-1 itself: the shipped keymap preset is vim-based and binds Ctrl+left-click to vim's <C-LeftMouse> (go to the tag under the click), so taking that chord would remove a working vim binding

C-TAB in the minibuffer runs file-cache-minibuffer-complete on the line being typed: it completes the file name from the file-name cache and, repeated, cycles through the directories that name was cached in. Reports [No match] for an uncached name and says so when the cache is empty

`t` in the Buffer Menu visits the buffer at point as a tags table (Buffer-menu-visit-tags-table): its file is parsed as an etags TAGS table and becomes the visited one for later tag lookups, or is refused with a message when it holds no etags entries

prompts for the spec, takes the fontset name from the FONTPATTERN before the first comma, records it and rejects a duplicate name with emacs's `Fontset "x" already exists`; describe-fontset then lists it. The fontset is bookkeeping only — the terminal emulator owns the single font it draws with, so no glyph rendering changes

lists the fontsets create-fontset-from-fontset-spec defined and the CHARSET/CHAR-RANGE -> FONT rows set-fontset-font recorded, in a scratch buffer; with nothing defined it reports emacs's tty message `No fontsets being used`. It cannot describe a real per-charset font table because a terminal has none

prompts for FONTSET TARGET FONT, requires the fontset to have been created (or `nil` for the default one) and records the assignment for describe-fontset. When the target is the default fontset's whole ASCII/latin/`t` range the font is also requested from the terminal with OSC 50, which xterm and rxvt honour; a narrower character target cannot be expressed to any terminal and is recorded only

prompts for the display and creates a real frame through Editor::new_frame (its own window tree, reachable with C-x 5 o), reporting the display it was asked for. The display argument cannot select anything: a zmax process is attached to one terminal, so every frame shares it, as in emacs -nw

prompts for the monitor and creates a real frame through Editor::new_frame, reporting the monitor it was asked for. Placing a frame on a chosen physical monitor needs a window system; the terminal emulator decides where its window lives
asks the terminal emulator to toggle full-screen with the xterm window-manipulation sequence CSI 10;2t, and tracks the state so the toggle round-trips on emulators that do not implement XTWINOPS
F11 runs toggle-frame-fullscreen in the emacs keymap preset (in the vim/spacemacs default F11 stays the debugger's step-in)
maximizes the terminal window with CSI 9;1t and restores it with CSI 9;0t; the maximized state is tracked so repeated invocations alternate
M-F10 runs toggle-frame-maximized in the emacs keymap preset

C-z runs iconify-or-deiconify-frame in the emacs keymap preset, which sends the XTWINOPS iconify (CSI 2t) and de-iconify (CSI 1t) requests to the terminal emulator. This is the windowed C-z; the tty C-z that suspends the process stays on the vim/spacemacs default preset's C-z

the C-x 5 frame prefix: 2 make-frame-command, 0 delete-frame, 1 delete-other-frames, o other-frame, b switch-to-buffer-other-frame, d dired-other-frame, f find-file-other-frame, r find-file-read-only-other-frame, u undelete-frame. Present in the vim/spacemacs default preset already; added to the emacs preset by this batch

turns the top tab strip on and off (the same strip tab-bar-mode drives). Emacs scopes this to the selected frame while other frames keep their own setting; zmax has one tab-bar switch shared by every frame, so switching frames does not restore a per-frame value

C-1 through C-8 select that numbered tab (`:tab-switch N`) in the emacs keymap preset. Control is the modifier the digits ship on because emacs's M-<digit> is digit-argument, which zmax reads in EditorView::handle_prefix_key
C-9 selects the last tab (tab-last), as tab-bar.el binds the 9 key rather than the ninth tab
C-0 switches to the most recently visited tab (tab-recent); pressing it again returns, so it toggles between the two

`:tab-bar-select-tab-modifiers meta` installs M-1 … M-8 as tab-select in normal, select and insert modes, exactly as customizing the variable defines those keys in emacs. It takes the previous modifier's digits back off first, and `nil` removes them; while meta is chosen M-<digit> stops being digit-argument, as it does in emacs
with `:tab-bar-select-tab-modifiers meta`, M-9 runs tab-last
with `:tab-bar-select-tab-modifiers meta`, M-0 runs tab-recent

turns on a menu-bar row at the top of the frame listing the File/Edit/Search/… titles; the row is taken out of the editor area, and clicking a title drops that menu down under it. Off by default (emacs -nw spends a row on it, zmax does not until asked); F10 / menu-bar-open reaches the same tree either way
with menu-bar-mode off, C-mouse-3 pops the menu bar's own tree up as a menu, so the menus stay reachable without a row. With the row showing, the binding is left alone, as in emacs

turns on a tool-bar row under the menu bar with the default tool-bar-map actions (New, Open, Save, Undo, Redo, Cut, Copy, Paste, Search, Replace); a terminal has no icons, so each button is its label, and clicking one runs the command it names

turns on a row of Ctrl/Meta/Shift/Super buttons under the tool bar. Clicking one latches that modifier, draws it lit, and applies it to exactly the next key the editor reads — the keyboards-without-modifiers case the mode exists for. Off by default, as in emacs

reserves the top row of each window for a tool bar of the buffer's verbs (Save, Undo, Redo, Format, Def, Refs, Diag), taken out of View::inner_area so the text really moves down; clicking a button focuses that window and runs the command. Emacs makes this mode buffer-local so only some windows get a bar — zmax's row is reserved in every window, which is what global-window-tool-bar-mode means
turns the per-window tool-bar row on in every window; the row is taken out of each window's text area (View::inner_area / inner_height), as emacs's window tool bar takes the tab-line row

toggles a one-column vertical scroll bar on the right edge of every window (emacs's default side), reserved out of View::inner_area so it is not drawn over text. The thumb is as tall a fraction of the bar as the window is of the buffer, at least one row, positioned at the same fraction down — emacs's own proportions

toggles the same vertical scroll bar. Emacs scopes toggle-scroll-bar to the selected frame; zmax has one scroll-bar setting shared by every frame and window, so it cannot be turned on for one frame and off for another

toggles a scroll-bar row on each window's bottom row, between the text and the mode line and reserved out of View::inner_area / inner_height. Its thumb shows how far right the window is scrolled against the widest column reached

pressing mouse-1 on the vertical scroll bar moves the window to that point in the buffer and keeps following the pointer until the button is released, even once it leaves the bar. The handler records the click as a fraction of the bar and dispatches through scroll-bar-drag, so the command really is the scroll bar's handler; point is pulled to the new top line when the scroll leaves it above the window

C-mouse-2 on the vertical scroll bar splits the window and puts the divider on the row that was clicked, so the top window keeps the lines above it — the manual's "the line of splitting goes through the place where you click"

controls the divider column drawn between side-by-side windows (`ui.window`, honouring vim `fillchars` `vert:`); with the mode off the two panes touch. On by default, since zmax has always drawn it. Stacked windows are separated by the mode line, as in emacs without a bottom divider

moves the text-scale amount by round(log(scale)/log(1.2)) — face-remap.el's text-scale-mode-step — clamped to text-scale-set's -20..20, and emits one OSC 50 font step per whole step so the terminal really resizes its font where it implements the sequence. The scale factor is the command's argument because no terminal reports a pinch gesture

C-wheel-up / C-wheel-down dispatch through this command, which enlarges on wheel-up (emacs's mouse-wheel-down-event) and shrinks on wheel-down via the OSC 50 font steps text-scale-increase/decrease use. Invoked from a key or M-x without a preceding wheel event it reports which gesture drives it
control+meta with the wheel runs global-text-scale-adjust with the wheel supplying its increment; wheel-up is the enlarging direction, matching mouse-wheel-scroll-amount's control-meta entry
control+meta with the wheel down runs global-text-scale-adjust in the shrinking direction

with the mode on, the terminal backend drops the bold attribute from any cell drawn in inverse video with both colours at their defaults — the check at the end of realize_tty_face in emacs's src/xfaces.c. A numeric prefix of zero turns it back off, as in emacs

Serializes the live window tree (Tree::shape() in zmax-view/src/tree.rs) to JSON: the split structure, each split's orientation and child weights, every window's file, and which window had focus. Written to the argument path, or ~/.config/zmax/gdb-window-configuration.json when called with none. Conversion and round-trip are unit-tested in zmax-term/src/gud.rs.

Reads a file written by :gdb-save-window-configuration, opens every file it names, and rebuilds the window tree with Tree::build_from_shape (splits, orientations, weights and focus restored). A leaf whose file no longer opens is dropped and the split it emptied collapses; if nothing opens the layout is left untouched and the command errors.

Removes an expression from the DAP watch list (zmax-term/src/gud.rs). :gdb-watch EXPR adds one (the identifier at the cursor with no argument); the watch buffer re-evaluates each expression through DAP `evaluate` on every refresh. `D` on a row of :gdb-watch-buffer deletes that row's expression. Errors when the named expression is not being watched.

`:gud-def NAME KEY TEMPLATE…` records the %-escaped command template (%f/%F/%d/%l/%e/%a/%p, expanded by gud_format_command) and binds `C-x C-a KEY` to `:gud-call NAME` through the runtime mapping overlay (keymap/vim_map.rs), so the binding is live immediately and survives a keymap-preset switch. `:gud-call NAME` expands the template and sends it to the comint debugger buffer if one is open, else evaluates it through the active DAP session. The older prompted `static:gud_def` records name+template without a key.

When on and a debug session is stopped, moving the mouse over an identifier in a source window evaluates it (DAP `evaluate` on the selected frame) and shows `name = value`; a name not in scope reports that instead. Wired into EditorView's MouseEventKind::Moved handler and re-queried only when the word under the pointer changes. The value goes to the echo area, which is where Emacs puts it when frame tooltips are unavailable — a terminal has no frame tooltips.

Switches the commit at point in the log buffer between the one-line summary it lists and its full entry (author, date, whole message, from `git show -s`), several commits at a time. Bound to Tab in MagitLog rather than RET, because RET there already opens the commit's diff.

Toggles the follow flag; while it is on, moving the cursor in the Occur buffer (n/p/j/k/arrows/Home/End) displays the hit in the source window without closing the list, which is what C-o does by hand. Emacs also applies it to the compilation and grep buffers; zmax's compilation list has no cursor-bearing buffer (`:next-error` walks it directly), so there the flag currently has no effect.

Chooses which error list `:next-error` / `:previous-error` / `:first-error` walk: `compilation` (the default, filled by :compile/:make), `quickfix`, `loclist` or `diagnostics`. Emacs names a buffer; zmax's lists each live in their own store, so the argument names the list. With no argument the current selection is reported. The three navigation commands dispatch on it.

Arms the one-shot filter that opens the next VC command's argv on the buffer's title line for editing before it runs (Enter runs it as edited, Esc cancels); a key that runs no git command drops the prefix, as Emacs's does. `!` in the status buffer arms the same flag; the typable arms it on the open status buffer by name.

gud-remove on its `C-c` key, in the `emacs` keymap preset (keymap/emacs.rs), which had no other claim on C-c C-d. dap_remove_breakpoint clears the breakpoint on the cursor line unconditionally (never sets one) and re-sends DAP setBreakpoints. In the shipped spacemacs preset C-c C-d is zmax's debug-launch, which is why the whole GUD map lives there on the C-x C-a alias (C-x C-a C-d).

git_diff now reads cx.prefix_arg() — Emacs's (interactive "P") — exactly as vc.el's `historic` argument works: with a prefix argument it prompts `vc-diff — older revision:` then `Newer revision (default: current source):` and shows `git diff OLD [NEW] -- <file>` for the current file; without one it opens the side-by-side buffer-vs-HEAD viewer. The prefix argument comes from `C-u` in the emacs preset (universal_argument) or `SPC u` in the spacemacs default.

The tree-wide half of the same mechanism: vc_root_diff with a prefix argument hands over to vc-root-version-diff, prompting for the two revisions and running `git diff OLD [NEW]` over the whole tree; without one it diffs the working tree against HEAD.

`D` in the GDB Breakpoints buffer (crate::ui::gdb::GdbBreakpoints, opened by :gdb-breakpoints-buffer) deletes the breakpoint on the cursor row from Editor::breakpoints and re-sends DAP setBreakpoints; on a row disabled by SPC it drops the parked breakpoint instead. The buffer is a modal Component, so the key is not expressible as a keymap entry — the evidence is the command that opens it and the equivalent cursor-line command.
`RET` in the GDB Breakpoints buffer is gdb-goto-breakpoint: it closes the buffer, opens the breakpoint's file and puts point on its line.

The middle mouse button on a row of the GDB Breakpoints buffer does the same as RET (gdb-goto-breakpoint): the clicked row becomes current and its source line is visited. Handled in the component's Event::Mouse arm on MouseEventKind::Down(MouseButton::Middle).

`SPC` in the GDB Breakpoints buffer is gdb-toggle-breakpoint's enable/disable: the breakpoint is withdrawn from the adapter (removed from Editor::breakpoints and setBreakpoints re-sent) but stays listed with `n` in the Enb column, and a second SPC re-arms it with its condition intact — gdb's `disable`/`enable`, not `delete`.
`D` on a row of the watch-expression buffer (crate::ui::gdb::GdbWatch, opened by :gdb-watch-buffer) is gdb-var-delete: it stops watching that expression and the list redraws without it.

`RET` on a watch row is gdb-edit-value: it prompts `gdb-edit-value — EXPR = ` and assigns the answer through DAP setExpression, falling back to an assignment `evaluate` when the adapter does not advertise supportsSetExpression. The new value shows on the next refresh.

`d` in the GDB Threads buffer (crate::ui::gdb::GdbThreads, opened by :gdb-threads-buffer) makes the thread on the cursor row current (DAP select-thread) and then shows its disassembly, gated on the adapter's supportsDisassembleRequest.
`f` in the GDB Threads buffer selects the thread on the cursor row and shows its call stack (the cached DAP stackTrace frames, selected frame marked).
`l` in the GDB Threads buffer selects the thread on the cursor row and shows the locals of its innermost frame (DAP scopes/variables).
`r` in the GDB Threads buffer selects the thread on the cursor row and shows its CPU registers; adapters that expose no Registers scope say so instead.

log-edit-previous-comment in the commit-message editor: cycles backward through log-edit-comment-ring, the messages committed earlier in this process, replacing the message body. Implemented in MagitCommit (zmax-term/src/ui/magit.rs).
log-edit-next-comment: the forward direction through the same comment ring, back toward the message that was being written.
log-edit-comment-search-backward: prompts for a substring and moves backward through the comment ring to the first message containing it; an empty answer reuses log-edit-last-comment-match.
log-edit-comment-search-forward: the same substring search through the comment ring in the forward direction.

TAB in a comint buffer running gdb (`M-x gud-gdb`) is now gud-gdb-complete-command instead of shell completion: it sends gdb's own `complete <line up to point>`, so gdb's candidates print in the buffer. NOT done: inserting a unique candidate into the input line. gdb's reply arrives asynchronously on the process's stdout, and the comint has no request/response channel to read it back on, so the in-place completion Emacs performs is missing. TAB in a non-gdb comint is unchanged (completion-at-point).

opens the newsreader: reads ~/.newsrc plus the ~/.newsrc-zmax killed/zombie sidecar, contacts the news server and merges its LIST ACTIVE into the group list, then shows the group buffer (zmax-term/src/ui/gnus.rs). Backend is NNTP over TCP (RFC 3977 MODE READER / LIST ACTIVE / GROUP / OVER / ARTICLE, std::net, zmax-term/src/gnus.rs) taken from $NNTPSERVER or the :gnus argument; with neither set it falls back to a local mbox spool at ~/News, one file per group. First run kills every group the user is not subscribed to; groups that appear later become zombies, as the manual specifies. Connect and LIST ACTIVE run on a blocking task so the editor does not stall.
writes the subscribed/unsubscribed groups and their read ranges back to ~/.newsrc, the killed and zombie lists to ~/.newsrc-zmax, and closes the reader. Also bound to q in the group buffer.

fetches the group's overview lines from the backend (NNTP OVER, falling back to XOVER; the local spool parses the mbox headers) and switches to the summary buffer with the cursor on the first unread article. Also bound to SPC in the group buffer.
the default listing: subscribed groups that still have unread articles, unread count computed from the server's article window minus the .newsrc read ranges. Also bound to l and A s.
lists every subscribed and unsubscribed group, and never killed or zombie ones. Also bound to L and A u.
lists the killed groups, read from the ~/.newsrc-zmax sidecar and from what C-k killed this session. Also bound to A k.
lists the zombie groups — the ones that appeared on the server since the last session. Also bound to A z.
moves the group-buffer cursor down to the next line whose group still has unread articles, reporting "No more unread newsgroups" when there is none. Also bound to n.
the same motion upwards. Also bound to p and to DEL.

kills the group on the current line: it leaves the l and L listings immediately and is omitted from ~/.newsrc when the reader saves, matching the manual's "killed groups are not recorded in the .newsrc file". Also bound to C-k.

toggles subscribed and unsubscribed; run on a killed or zombie group it makes the group unsubscribed instead, as the manual states. The listing is recomputed so the group moves in or out of the current view. Also bound to u.

all three documented behaviours: with no article selected it selects the article on the summary line and displays it (marking it read), with one selected it scrolls the article pane a screenful, and at the end of the article it selects the next unread one. Also bound to SPC in the summary buffer.
scrolls the selected article backwards by a screenful. Also bound to DEL in the summary buffer.
fetches and displays the next article the group's read ranges do not cover, marks it read and moves the summary cursor onto it. Also bound to n in the summary buffer.
the same, scanning backwards from the summary cursor. Also bound to p in the summary buffer.

opens an inline I-search over the displayed article: each typed character re-scans the article's rendered lines case-insensitively and scrolls the article pane to the first hit, DEL shortens the pattern, RET keeps the position and Esc restores the scroll it started from. Refuses when no article is selected. Also bound to s in the summary buffer.

prompts for a regexp and walks the articles after the summary cursor, testing the overview subject/from first and then the fetched article text, and selects the first match. Uses the `regex` crate, case-insensitive. Also bound to M-s M-s in the summary buffer.
the same search walking backwards from the summary cursor. Also bound to M-s M-r and to a bare M-r in the summary buffer.

SPC in the Gnus group buffer opens the summary buffer for the group on the current line; the arm is in the View::Group key match of zmax-term/src/ui/gnus.rs and runs the same code as the gnus_group_read_group command cited here. The report parses component keymaps only for the modes named in gen_port_report.py, which has no `gnus` mode, so the command is cited instead of key:gnus:space.
l in the Gnus group buffer switches to the default listing (subscribed groups with unread articles); the arm is in zmax-term/src/ui/gnus.rs and runs the cited command. A s is bound to the same thing.
A is a prefix in the group buffer (pending_a in zmax-term/src/ui/gnus.rs); A s selects the subscribed-with-unread listing, the same as l.
L in the Gnus group buffer lists all subscribed and unsubscribed groups (never killed or zombie); the arm is in zmax-term/src/ui/gnus.rs and runs the cited command.
A u under the group buffer's A prefix selects the all-groups listing, the same as L.
A k under the group buffer's A prefix lists the killed groups; the arm is in zmax-term/src/ui/gnus.rs and runs the cited command.
A z under the group buffer's A prefix lists the zombie groups; the arm is in zmax-term/src/ui/gnus.rs and runs the cited command.
u in the Gnus group buffer toggles the group's subscription, turning a killed or zombie group into an unsubscribed one; the arm is in zmax-term/src/ui/gnus.rs and runs the cited command.
C-k in the Gnus group buffer kills the group on the current line, which then drops out of the l and L listings and out of ~/.newsrc; the arm is in zmax-term/src/ui/gnus.rs and runs the cited command.
n in the Gnus group buffer moves to the next group with unread articles; the arm is in zmax-term/src/ui/gnus.rs and runs the cited command.
p in the Gnus group buffer moves to the previous group with unread articles; the arm is in zmax-term/src/ui/gnus.rs and runs the cited command.
DEL in the Gnus group buffer is the same previous-unread-group motion as p; both Backspace and Delete are matched in zmax-term/src/ui/gnus.rs.

q in the Gnus group buffer saves ~/.newsrc and the killed/zombie sidecar and quits the reader; a failed write leaves the reader open with the error on the status line. The arm is in zmax-term/src/ui/gnus.rs and runs the cited command.

SPC in the Gnus summary buffer selects the article on the line, or scrolls the selected one, or moves to the next unread article at its end; the arm is in the View::Summary key match of zmax-term/src/ui/gnus.rs and runs the cited command.
DEL in the Gnus summary buffer scrolls the article backwards; Backspace and Delete are both matched in zmax-term/src/ui/gnus.rs.
n in the Gnus summary buffer selects the next unread article; the arm is in zmax-term/src/ui/gnus.rs and runs the cited command.
p in the Gnus summary buffer selects the previous unread article; the arm is in zmax-term/src/ui/gnus.rs and runs the cited command.
s in the Gnus summary buffer starts the incremental search over the selected article's text; the arm is in zmax-term/src/ui/gnus.rs and runs the cited command.
M-s is a prefix in the summary buffer (pending_meta_s in zmax-term/src/ui/gnus.rs); M-s M-s prompts for a regexp and selects the next article that matches.
M-s M-r under the summary buffer's M-s prefix prompts for a regexp and selects the previous article that matches; a bare M-r is bound to the same thing.

q in the Gnus summary buffer returns to the group buffer with this session's read marks applied, so a fully-read group leaves the default listing; the arm is in zmax-term/src/ui/gnus.rs and runs the cited command.
v in the Rmail reader toggles the decoded MIME display (rmail-mime): the message's entities are listed with TAB/S-TAB moving between them and RET showing or collapsing the one at point.

reports the weekly Torah reading. The Hebrew-calendar arithmetic is the port of cal-hebrew.el's diary-hebrew-parasha in zmax_core::diary::hebrew_parasha — the year's keviah (Rosh Hashanah weekday, complete/incomplete/regular year, Passover weekday) selects one of the fourteen reading tables and the Saturday's offset from the year's first Saturday indexes it, with the Diaspora/Israel split rendered as "A (Israel B)". The command reports today's reading on a Saturday and the coming Saturday's otherwise, and says so when a festival displaces the parasha. The %%(diary-hebrew-parasha) sexp entry already fired from the diary; this adds the interactive command.

collects the diary entries falling in the next diary-mail-days days, formats them per day in the current date style with each day's entries sorted by time, and opens a message-mode draft addressed to the user with subject "Diary entries generated MONTH DAY, YEAR". Reports that there is nothing to send when the window holds no entries.

prompts for SYMBOL COMPOSEFUNC SENDFUNC [ABORTFUNC HOOKVAR] and runs the four `put`s that define a mail user agent against the embedded elisp interpreter's symbol-plist, so (get 'AGENT 'sendfunc) reads the value back and mail-user-agent can name the agent. ABORTFUNC defaults to kill-buffer and HOOKVAR to mail-send-hook, as in Emacs.
runs the `fortune` program and inserts its output as the RFC 3676 signature block at point in the draft; reports the failure when fortune is not installed or produces nothing.

opens the *Help* buffer — zmax's Help browser — and reports its Help-mode keys; when one is already open (as its own layer or as the Preferences page's Help tab) it only re-reports, since turning a major mode on in its own buffer does nothing. The mode's keys are live in that buffer: RET help-follow, TAB/S-TAB forward/backward-button, l or C-c C-b and r or C-c C-f the history, n/p the pages, s help-view-source.

follows the cross-reference at point: every Help row is a cross-reference to its entry, so this visits the selected one, shows it on its own and pushes it onto the history help-go-back/help-go-forward walk. Errors 'No cross-reference here' when point is on no row, and 'No *Help* window' when no help buffer is open.

moves to the Nth next button with the interactive WRAP and DISPLAY-MESSAGE arguments: past the last button it continues from the first, and the button's help-echo is echoed. In the Help buffer the buttons are its rows; in a document they are the regions zmax can act on — a URL (browse-url), an existing path (find-file), and, only in a buffer with no file behind it (a *Help*/report buffer, where emacs has its symbol hyperlinks), a command name. Scanner and motion in zmax-term/src/emacs_button.rs; errors 'No buttons!'.
forward-button with a negated count, as button.el defines it: the Nth previous button, wrapping from the first to the last and echoing the button's help-echo.

shows a buffer reporting the type and action of the button under point (button.el reports type/action/mouse-action): a URL is a link whose action is browse-url, an existing path a file visited by find-file, a command name a command that is run. Errors 'No button at point'.

shows a buffer reporting the type and action of the Customize widget under point: the option named by the symbol at point, its widget type (toggle for a boolean, number/editable/sexp field otherwise) and its set-option action. Errors 'No widget at point'.

moves the widget cursor of the customization buffer (the Preferences Settings page) to the next button or editable field, wrapping. The widget sequence is the header buttons [Apply], [Apply and Save], raw config.toml and close, followed by every visible option field; the focused button is drawn in the accent colour and RET activates whichever widget holds the cursor.
the same widget cursor stepped backwards, wrapping from the first button to the last field.

completes the value of the customization field at point from the option's value set, following the completion-in-region contract: a unique match is inserted whole ('Sole completion: x'), several extend the text to their longest common prefix and are then listed ('Complete, but not unique: …'), and a field with no completion table reports 'No completions available for this field'. An enum field that is not being edited is opened for editing first.

sets the edited setting of the customization buffer for the current session only: the value goes into the running editor config (ConfigEvent::Update, the same path :set uses) and is recorded in the session-customization store as SET-but-unsaved (marked '*' in the buffer); config.toml is not touched. With nothing edited it reports 'No edited settings in this buffer', matching custom-command-apply having no modified widget to act on.

sets the edited setting, then writes every option set this session into ~/.zmax/config.toml under [editor] — zmax's custom file — parsing the existing file and replacing only those keys, and clears their SET-but-unsaved state. Reports how many were saved, or 'No customizations to save'.

asks 'Some customized options have not been saved; Examine? (yes or no) ' and, on a spelled-out yes (yes-or-no-p), opens the buffer listing each option set this session with its saved and session value; with nothing unsaved it says so instead. The same query runs on C-x C-c in the customization buffer.

echoes the help text of the active text at point: the message of the diagnostic covering point (a language server's help-echo), else the help-echo of the button there ('mouse-1, RET: browse-url — open <url>' / 'find-file — visit <path>' / 'run the command `x`'), else 'No local help at point'.

runs help-view-source in the *Help* buffer from anywhere: resolves the help item being displayed to its `fn <name>(` definition by walking the workspace sources (gitignore-honouring) and opens that file at the line. Errors 'Source file for the current help item is not defined' when the item has none (a typable :command, an alias or a topic page), and 'No *Help* window' when no help buffer is open.

picks a command (the describe-command picker) and shows the manual node `info --index-search=<command> emacs` finds for it, reporting emacs' own "Couldn't find documentation for X" when the command index has no entry.
reads a key sequence through the describe-key picker (bindings searched by their key sequence), then shows the manual node the command index has for the command that key runs.

looks the file name at point (info-look's file character class, or the selection) up in the (libc)File Index via `info --index-search` and shows the node; reports 'Not documented as a file: X' when the index has no entry. The prompt offers the name at point as the default.

shows the incremental-search help buffer: every isearch-* command with the chord the live keymap binds it to (or M-x when unbound) and its documentation, read from the command table and the live reverse keymap so it cannot go stale — the isearch-describe-bindings/isearch-describe-mode content of the map. NOT done: it is not reachable as C-h C-h from inside the search prompt (run it as a command), and the map's other entries are not separate sub-commands.

prompts 'Show summary for functions in: ' with completion over the areas of interest (buffer, file, window, search, edit, selection, lsp, shell, register) and pops a buffer listing that area's commands, each with its live documentation and the example invocation. Groups are in zmax-term/src/emacs_shortdoc.rs; every description is read from the command tables at render time, and a group naming a command that does not exist is a test failure.

switches the active theme to another variant: with a single sibling it switches straight to it, with several it prompts with completion, and with none it errors 'No other variant of theme `X`'. A theme's variants are the installed themes that differ from it only in a light/dark name segment, separator style ignored — ayu_dark↔ayu_light, adwaita-dark↔adwaita_light, github_dark_colorblind↔github_light_colorblind, gruvbox↔gruvbox_light (zmax-term/src/emacs_custom.rs, unit-tested). Exactly one theme is ever enabled, so emacs' 'only works if a single theme is active' precondition always holds; the switch is for this session and custom-theme-save persists it.
TAB in the Help buffer is forward-button: point moves to the next hyperlink and wraps from the last to the first, as the manual says these commands act cyclically.
S-TAB in the Help buffer is backward-button: point moves to the previous hyperlink, wrapping from the first to the last.

TAB in the customization buffer runs widget-forward: the Settings page's widget cursor moves to the next button or editable field, wrapping. Real key, handled in ui/preferences.rs and ui/settings.rs; the report parser exposes no mode for that component, so the command it runs is the citable token.

S-TAB in the customization buffer runs widget-backward, the same widget cursor stepped backwards. Real key, handled in ui/preferences.rs and ui/settings.rs; no parsed mode exposes that component's keys, so the command is the citable token.

M-TAB in the customization buffer runs widget-complete on the field being edited (ui/settings.rs matches a raw ALT|Tab KeyEvent). Real key; no parsed mode exposes that component's keys, so the command is the citable token.
C-M-i is the other encoding of the same key and is matched as a raw CONTROL|ALT 'i' KeyEvent in ui/settings.rs, so it runs widget-complete exactly like M-TAB.

C-c C-c in the customization buffer is Custom-set: a real two-key chord (C-c arms a prefix in ui/settings.rs, as an emacs prefix key does) that sets the edited setting for the current session without writing config.toml. The [Apply] button runs the same command.

the manual's index anchor at this node is `C-x C-c (customization buffer)` while the prose it marks reads "The command C-x C-s (Custom-save) is like using the [Save for Future Sessions] button" (custom.texi has @kindex C-x C-c next to @kindex C-c C-c for that paragraph). Both keys are live in zmax's customization buffer: C-x C-s runs Custom-save, and C-x C-c leaves the buffer through the custom-prompt-customize-unsaved-options query, which is what C-x C-c does in emacs with that hook installed. Real two-key chords, armed by the C-x prefix in ui/settings.rs.

C-x C-s in the Color Scheme page (zmax's *Custom Themes* buffer) is custom-theme-save: it writes the enabled theme into config.toml as `theme = "<name>"`, preserving every other key, so future sessions start with it. Picking a theme from the list now enables it for the current session only and is marked '*' until saved; the [Save Theme Settings] button runs the same thing. Real two-key chord, armed by the C-x prefix in ui/theme_editor.rs.

mouse-2 is push-button: a middle click on a Help row follows that cross-reference (ui/help.rs handle_mouse), and a click on a customization-buffer button or field activates it. NOT done: an ordinary document has no clickable buttons — the URL/path/command regions forward-button walks are not activated by a click there.

mouse-1 activates a button through follow-link, so a left click on a Help row follows the cross-reference and a left click on a customization-buffer button or field activates it (ui/help.rs, ui/settings.rs). NOT done: in an ordinary document a left click only moves point — the button regions forward-button walks are not clickable there.

emacs image-next-frame (f): steps to the Nth frame after the current one, default 1, negative N stepping backwards. The terminal viewers take whole files rather than frame indices, so ex_image_next_frame decodes the selected frame out to a temporary file with the same ImageMagick the transform path already shells out to; the selected index is held per-image in IMAGE_ANIM.
emacs image-previous-frame (b): the same frame stepper as image-next-frame with the sign inverted, decoding the chosen frame to a temporary file for the terminal viewer.
emacs image-goto-frame: selects an absolute frame of the animation and redisplays it, storing the 0-based index in IMAGE_ANIM so the frame steppers continue from it.

emacs image-increase-speed (a +): doubles the image-animate-speed multiplier. A speed change is applied by re-encoding the animation's per-frame delays, since the terminal viewers play a file rather than accept a rate.
emacs image-decrease-speed (a -): halves the image-animate-speed multiplier, re-encoding the animation's per-frame delays the same way image-increase-speed does.

emacs image-reset-speed (a 0): resets the speed's magnitude to 1 while keeping direction, matching image--set-speed's `reset` symbol, which resolves to -1 when the animation runs backwards and 1 otherwise — a reversed image stays reversed and only its rate returns to the file's own delays.
emacs image-reverse-speed (a r): plays the animation the other way round while keeping its rate, matching image--set-speed multiplying the speed by -1.

emacs doc-view-show-tooltip: shows doc-view-current-info (the 'Page N of M.' string built in doc-view-goto-page). Emacs pops a GUI tooltip; on a tty its own tooltip-show has no frame to draw into and falls back to the echo area, which is where zmax puts it — the status line.

writes the image's data — the file's own bytes, or a pending image-crop/image-cut result — to a named file; rotation, flip and scale are display state and are deliberately not baked in, matching image.el's "rotating or changing the displayed image size does not affect the saved image". `i o` prompts "Write image to file:"; the typable takes the path as its argument.

marks the visited file in Dired's listing of its directory. A Dired overlay already on the compositor for that directory is marked in place; otherwise the mark is recorded per-directory and Dired::new seeds a fresh listing from it, which is the observable effect of Emacs marking a background Dired buffer. Errors with Emacs's "Current buffer is not visiting a file" when there is no file.
clears the mark set by image-mode-mark-file, through the same per-directory table and live-Dired update.

prompts for `SUFFIX COMMAND` and registers COMMAND as the converter for files with that suffix; the display pipeline runs it with the source file as $1 and renders the PNG it writes to stdout. Registering a suffix also makes is_image_path accept it, which is what image-converter-file-name-extensions does. An empty COMMAND removes the handler.

builds the contact sheet with ImageMagick montage — every image in the directory scaled into a 100px cell (thumbs-thumbsize), 4 per row (thumbs-per-line), labelled with its file name — and shows it in the terminal. Not done: thumbs.el's cursor over the grid, so there is no RET/`SPC` to open the thumbnail at point and no per-thumbnail marking; and no thumbnail cache directory. Needs ImageMagick's `montage`.

reads the clipboard's image/png (pngpaste, else AppleScript's «class PNGf», on macOS; wl-paste under Wayland, xclip under X11), saves it beside the buffer's file as -.png and inserts the reference the buffer's language uses — markdown ![](f), org [[file:f]], html , latex \includegraphics{f}, rst, asciidoc, typst — which is zmax's stand-in for the yank-media-handler registry. Not done: only image/png is read; Emacs's text/html and image/* variants other than PNG are not, and a language with no registered handler gets the bare path inserted rather than Emacs's "no handler" error.

renders the current page, turns on SGR mouse reporting and reads two mouse-1 presses, converts the two clicked cells to page pixels, then stores the slice and redisplays the page cropped to it; subsequent pages keep the slice, and `c r` (doc-view-reset-slice) clears it. Two presses rather than Emacs's press-and-drag, because the page is drawn by an external viewer while zmax's terminal is released, so the clicks are decoded by the same foreground script. Needs chafa (its --stretch --size makes the cell-to-pixel mapping exact) and ImageMagick identify.

lays the buffer out on handwrite.el's own page — origin (handwrite-xstart 30, handwrite-ystart 810), handwrite-linespace 12 leading, handwrite-numlines 60 lines per page, handwrite-fontsize 11, page number drawn at (20, 30) — shows the PostScript in a buffer (Emacs's *handwrittenN.ps*) and pipes it to lpr. Not done: the glyphs are Courier-Oblique, not Emacs's embedded "Joepie" Type 3 handwriting font, whose hand-drawn outlines zmax does not ship.

opens the printing package's front-end as a picker whose rows are printing.el's buttons — ps-print-buffer, ps-print-region, ps-print-buffer-with-faces, ps-spool-buffer, ps-spool-region, ps-despool, handwrite — and choosing a row runs that command against the current buffer. Not done: it is a picker, not printing.el's Widget form, so the scope radio buttons are folded into separate rows instead of being a mode; and only the PostScript printer section is offered, not the text-printer or the printer/ppd selection widgets.

prompts for a URL (or takes it as an argument), prepends https:// to a bare host as Emacs does, fetches it and renders it into a buffer with the same HTML-to-text renderer zmax's eww uses, then puts the Xwidget-WebKit keymap over that buffer. Not the real thing: this is a text render, not an embedded WebKit widget — no JavaScript, no CSS layout, no images, no form submission or link activation.

puts the WebKit buffer's one-key command map over the current buffer (g browse-url, r reload, b/f back/forward, w current-url, H browse-history, e edit-mode, C-s/C-r isearch-mode, q quit) and takes it off again when re-run, the way image-mode doubles as its own toggle. Not the real thing: it is a keymap over a text-rendered page, not the major mode of a live WebKit widget, so xwidget-webkit-scroll-*, zoom and adjust-size have no widget to act on and are not bound — ordinary buffer motions scroll the page instead.

displays a buffer listing this session's page loads, oldest first, with the page on screen marked — the *Xwidget WebKit History* buffer. The list is the same back-forward list xwidget-webkit-back/-forward walk, and a fresh load from the middle of it truncates the entries ahead, as a browser does.

toggles the mode that decides where keystrokes go: while it is on the viewer stops consuming self-inserting characters and they reach the buffer holding the page, instead of running the mode's one-key commands; Esc turns it off. That is Emacs's contract for the mode, but the destination differs — there is no live WebKit widget, so the characters land in the rendered text rather than in a web form.

an incremental search over the page: typing extends the query and moves the cursor to the match, C-s shows the next result and C-r the previous one, both wrap, the prompt reads "failing" when there is no match, and RET/Esc exit. Not the real thing: it searches the rendered text, not the WebKit widget's own find machinery, so matches in content the text renderer drops (alt text, script, hidden elements) are not found and results are not highlighted in a page layout.

image-crop: reads an ImageMagick WxH+X+Y region in the viewer's minibuffer and runs image-crop.el's image-crop-crop-command (`+repage -crop WxH+X+Y`) over the image; the result is a pending, unsaved edit that `i o` (image-save) writes out. The region is typed rather than dragged as an SVG rubber band, since the picture is painted into the terminal by an external viewer.
image-save: prompts "Write image to file:" and copies the image's data — the file's bytes, or a pending crop/cut result — to that path, leaving the display transforms out of the saved file.

image-transform-reset-to-initial: clears rotation, both flips and the scale back to the size the image was first displayed at. In Emacs this differs from `s o` (-reset-to-original) only in restoring image-auto-resize rather than no resize; the terminal viewer always fits the picture to the window, so both land on the same state here and share a handler.

image-transform-set-percent: reads "Scale (% of original): " in the viewer's minibuffer and redisplays the image resized to that percentage of its original size; a non-positive value is rejected with Emacs's "Not a positive number".
image-transform-set-scale: reads "Scale: " and resizes the image by that multiplier (1.5 = 150%), redisplaying at the new scale.

prompts for one of the registered Quail packages (latin-1-prefix, latin-1-postfix, japanese-hiragana, chinese-py-b5, russian-computer, TeX) with completion and makes it the buffer's input method; typed keys are then translated by that package's rule table before self-insert sees them. current-input-method is per-document, so a second buffer is unaffected.

turns the buffer's input method off when one is active and back on when none is, remembering the last one as default-input-method; with nothing ever selected, or with a prefix argument, it prompts like set-input-method. Because deactivating drops the half-typed key sequence, C-\ C-\ between two characters stops them combining, as the manual describes. The shipped vim/spacemacs preset keeps vim's CTRL-\ CTRL-N prefix on C-\, so the key binding is in the emacs preset; the command itself runs from M-x in every preset.

enables an input method for exactly one inserted chunk and then restores whatever method was active before; the method is read from the minibuffer the first time and remembered as default-transient-input-method, and a prefix argument (C-u C-x \) asks again.

lists every Quail package with its language, its mode-line indicator and its rule count, marking the one the buffer is using. The typable also lists the vim keymaps in the 'runtimepath', which :set keymap= loads as Lang-Arg tables.

shows the package's mode-line indicator, its docstring and its whole key table in a scratch buffer; with no name it describes the method the buffer is using, and it accepts any registered package name without activating it. C-h I is bound to the same command.

prompts for one of quail-keyboard-layout-alist's layouts (standard, sun-type3, atari-german, pc102-de, jp106, pc105-uk) with completion and records it as quail-keyboard-layout-type. Not done: no ported package is layout-dependent — all six translate character sequences, not physical key positions — so the stored layout has no effect on translation yet.

reverse-looks-up the character after point in the active method's rule table and reports "To input 'X', type \"keys\"", or quail's "Such key sequence to input 'X' not found". For a candidate method a key counts when the character is one of the alternatives it offers, so it finds the pinyin spellings of a han character. The typable falls back to the vim Lang-Arg table when no Quail package is active.

the keymap that overrides the ordinary one while a translation is being chosen, with quail.el's own default bindings (C-f/C-b/right/left next-prev translation, C-n/C-p/down/up translation block, TAB completion, C-SPC and C-@ select-current, DEL delete-last-char). :quail-translation-keymap lists it, :quail-translation-keymap KEY COMMAND rebinds a key and :quail-translation-keymap KEY unbinds it, which is emacs's documented (keymap-set (quail-translation-keymap) …). Rebinding takes effect immediately: the insert-mode key path consults this table before the keymap.

toggle-input-method. Bound in the emacs preset's insert and normal maps; the shipped vim/spacemacs preset leaves C-\ as vim's CTRL-\ CTRL-N prefix, where the command is reached by M-x toggle-input-method instead.
activate-transient-input-method: the method translates one chunk and then switches itself off again, restoring the previous method.
set-input-method, grafted onto the existing C-x RET coding-system map rather than replacing it.
describe-input-method — the package's documentation and full key table. C-h I runs the same command.

quail-next-translation: while a Chinese method is showing a row of alternatives, C-f moves to the next one, replacing the character in the buffer and re-drawing the echo-area row with it highlighted; it stops at the end of the list. The translation keymap is consulted before the ordinary keymap (emacs's overriding-terminal-local-map), so C-f is forward-char again the moment the translation region closes.
quail-prev-translation: the previous alternative in the current row, stopping at its start; otherwise C-b is backward-char.

quail-next-translation-block: the next row of ten alternatives, keeping the position within the row; the echo area's (i/j) counter follows. Refused on the last row. Otherwise C-n is the ordinary binding.
quail-prev-translation-block: the previous row of ten, refused on the first row.

quail-completion: TAB shows every alternative of the current key sequence at once, in rows of ten with the current one bracketed, in a popup that does not take point out of the buffer being typed into; while it is up C-f/C-b/C-n/C-p and the digits move the highlight in the listing instead of in the echo area, and it comes down when the translation ends. Not done: mouse-2 does not choose an alternative from the listing.

moves to the character to the left on display: backward through the buffer in a left-to-right paragraph and forward in a right-to-left one, with the paragraph's base direction determined dynamically by UAX #9's P2/P3 rule (zmax-core/src/bidi.rs). With :visual-order-cursor-movement on it instead steps one screen position, using the line's logical-to-visual reordering, so it crosses a reversed Hebrew or Arabic run one glyph at a time and moves to the neighbouring line at the visual edge. The reordering implements the implicit UBA rules (levels, numbers, neutral resolution, L2 run reversal); the explicit embedding and isolate controls are treated as neutrals.
the mirror of left-char: forward through the buffer in a left-to-right paragraph, backward in a right-to-left one, or one screen position to the right when :visual-order-cursor-movement is on.

reports every category the character after point belongs to, from the real category table (zmax-core/src/category.rs) ported from characters.el and kinsoku.el — the script categories, the computed ones (base, combining, digit, strong-L2R/R2L) and the fill categories — each with what the category means. Emacs's per-buffer table is one shared standard table here.
renders the category set of the character after point as the string of its mnemonics, e.g. the Lisp manual's own (category-set-mnemonics (char-category-set ?a)) example, whose set contains a and l.

adds a character to a category or, with a prefix argument / the `reset` argument, removes it; the typable also takes a range (A-Z, U+4E00-U+9FFF), which is emacs's (min . max) cons. The change is live: line breaking reads the table, so putting a character into `|` makes auto-fill break beside it and putting one into `>` stops a line ever starting with it (commands.rs fill_break_point, emacs's fill-find-break-point / kinsoku).

:standard-display-8bit LOW HIGH installs the 8-bit display table and marks codes LOW..HIGH printable, so they render as the characters they stand for; every other single-byte code the table calls unprintable keeps rendering as an escape, which is emacs's default treatment of 128-159. Implemented over the same table `:set isprint` uses (zmax-core/src/graphemes.rs set_printable_range), so the effect is on the drawn glyphs, not on the buffer contents.

emacs C-u TAB (indent-for-tab-command with a numeric argument). indent_sexp_rigidly (commands.rs) already reindented the current line with the tree-sitter indent and shifted every other line of the parenthetical grouping starting on it by that same delta, leaving lines that start inside a string alone; it was registered but unreachable from a key. smart_tab now tests cx.prefix_arg() before indent-line-function and dispatches to it, so TAB under a prefix argument is the grouping shifter whatever function plain TAB would run — matching the Multi-line Indent manual node: 'TAB with a numeric argument reindents the current line as usual, then reindents by the same amount all the lines in the parenthetical grouping starting on the current line.' TAB reaches smart_tab through the emacs preset's tab -> emmet_expand, which falls back to it.

opens the *abbrev-suggest* report built by emacs_abbrev::suggest_show_report() — the header plus ` EXPANSION: COUNT` for every expansion typed by hand that an abbrev covers, tallied by abbrev--suggest-maybe-suggest as you type; the buffer's major mode is set to abbrev-suggest

reads `NAME question…` and registers the question against the command; MappableCommand::execute then asks it (y/n, or yes/no with a universal argument) before running that command however it was invoked — key, M-x or macro — and a `y` lets it through exactly once. A name with no question takes the query off again

sets the comment column to the cursor's display column; with a universal argument it takes the column from the nearest comment above and realigns this line's comment under it. C-x ; now runs it instead of the generated command-palette fallback

reads `PROFILE var=value var=value…` and stores the profile in emacs_misc; redeclaring a profile replaces it. Profiles are looked up per connection by emacs_misc::variables_for once connection-local-set-profiles has activated them

reads `:machine host :protocol ssh :user name PROFILE…`, rejects undeclared profiles, and activates the profiles for every connection the criteria matches (a criteria naming nothing matches every remote directory, as nil does). Connections are parsed from Tramp-style paths (/ssh:user@host:/path) by emacs_misc::Connection::from_path and the resolved values are readable with variables_for/variable_for; no zmax subsystem consumes a connection-local value yet, so setting shell-file-name for a remote host stores and resolves but does not yet change which shell runs

dumps the internal state at point — mode, primary selection, cursor char/byte/line/column, the character at point and the syntax node under it — to the log and a *Debug* scratch buffer, the analogue of printing a Lisp object's reader representation from the debugger
reads one key and inserts its name into the macro text in the correct format, on a line of its own at column 0 and space-separated otherwise, as edmacro.el does

pops the innermost recursive editing level (emacs_misc::recursive_enter/exit keeps the nesting stack) and reports how many are still open; errors with `No recursive edit is in progress` at top level. Leaving a level opened by C-r at a kbd-macro-query asks the query again

rgrep/lgrep/grep-find now append the grep-find-ignored-directories list (SCCS RCS CVS .svn .git .hg .bzr _darcs node_modules target …) as rg --glob exclusions and record the command as (head, ignored); the command shown when the grep starts hides the ignore list behind `…` while grep-find-abbreviate is on. This command flips it and re-prints the last command in the new form

prompts (with completion) for indent-according-to-mode, indent-relative or insert-tab and stores it; smart_tab consults it first, so TAB really indents with the chosen function and falls through to zmax's syntax-aware indent for the default

toggles the input method used for the search string — zmax's input method is the vim Lang-Arg table (:lmap, :set keymap=…) and 'imsearch' is the switch that gates it on the search line, which is what this flips

prompts for the name of an installed input method (the keymap/{name}.vim files on the runtimepath, completed), loads it and turns 'imsearch' on so the search string is typed through it; an empty name deactivates.
